Kennedy gave a speech before a joint session of Congress, committing the nation to achieve the goal of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth before the end of the decade. NASA’s Space Task Group, in charge of America’s human spaceflight program, was already working on Project Mercury to put astronauts into Earth orbit, but with the additional task of a human lunar landing, it soon outgrew its facilities at NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia. The agency decided it needed a dedicated field center for human spaceflight and on Sept. 19, 1961, after evaluating multiple sites around the country, NASA announced that the new Manned Spacecraft Center would be built near Houston, Texas. The agency established the center on Nov. 1, 1961, and construction began in 1962. In 1973, it officially became NASA’s Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center in honor of President Johnson for his ardent support of America’s space program from its foundation. Manned Spacecraft Center to Johnson Space Center The Manned Spacecraft Center officially opened on Nov. 1, 1961, and while construction continued on the Clear Lake site, employees worked in 13 leased buildings in southeast Houston. The design phase took six months and construction of the first buildings took 18 months, with the first employees moving onto the new site in late 1963. Over the decades, the number of buildings grew, and continues to grow, to meet the demands of new spaceflight programs. View of the Manned Spacecraft Center during construction in 1963. Aerial view of NASA’s Johnson Space Center and Space Center Houston in 2025. NASA/James Blair Project Management Building Construction of the nine-story Project Management Building began on Dec. 5, 1962, and concluded on March 15, 1964. Robert Gilruth , the center’s first director, moved into his office on March 5, 1964, on the top floor of the edifice then known as Building 2. The building swapped numbers with the Public Affairs Building, originally known as Building 1, on June 30, 1974. The main administration building, called Building 2 until 1974, during President Richard Nixon’s visit in 1974. Employees pose for a group photo in front of Building 1 in 2024. NASA/Robert Markowitz Photo taken in 1964 from the main administration building toward the city of Nassau Bay. The same view from roughly the same vantage point in 2026, showing the mature oak trees and the extensive development outside the center’s gates. Neutral buoyancy spacewalk training The use of neutral buoyancy for spacewalk training began with the Gemini XII mission in 1966. In 1967, workers installed an above-ground circular pool called the Water Immersion Facility for astronaut training that supported Apollo and pre-Shuttle spacewalk training.. To accommodate the larger size of the space shuttle payload bay, spacewalk training moved to the Weightless Environment Training Facility iin 1980. Astronauts used it for nearly all shuttle spacewalk training until 1997, when the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in the Sonny Carter Training Center entered operations for both shuttle and space station training, as well as testing future space suits and lunar surface activities. Astronaut candidate Anna L. Fisher trains at the Water Immersion Facility in Houston in 1979. Exploration geologists and Artemis science officers Trevor Graff, left, and Angela Garcia carry out a lunar training development run at NASA’s Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory (NBL) in Houston. This testing run marked the first time in the Artemis program that two geologists were suited up simultaneously for lunar geology training in the NBL. Lunar Receiving Laboratory (Building 37) To prevent any back contamination from any possible lunar microorganisms, NASA designed the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in Building 37. Construction began in August 1966, with the first employees moving into their offices in June 1967. The astronauts from Apollo 11, 12, and 14 completed their three-week postflight quarantine in the lab, and scientists in the various laboratories studied the lunar samples all the Apollo missions returned. Following the Apollo program, Life Sciences division and laboratories moved into the building until they relocated in 2017. Following demolition of Building 37, the Lunar Receiving Park, dedicated in 2026, honors the history of the laboratory. Building 37 that housed the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in May 1969, two months before the first Moon landing. Aerial view of the Lunar Receiving Park built on the site of Building 37 in 2026. NASA/Robert Markowitz A scientist views an Apollo 11 Moon rock at the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in 1969. Spacecraft mockup training facilities (Building 9) Construction of Building 9 began in December 1965 and finished in March 1967. The building initially housed the Technical Services Facility. In April 1969, workers converted a portion of the building to include a mock lunar surface scene, complete with a mockup of a Lunar Module, used by Apollo 11 astronauts. To support the space shuttle program, workers completed an addition that housed the Mockup and Integration Laboratory in September 1974. Astronauts for all 135 shuttle missions used the mockups for training. An extension on the northwest side of thebuilding begun in 1986 and completed in 1988. It received mockups of Space Station Freedom and later of the International Space Station, and the building was renamed the Space Vehicle Mockup Facility. Today, the facility also houses training mockups of NASA’s Orion spacecraft, commercial mockups, and the Active Response Gravity Offload System, known as ARGOS. Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong, left, and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin train for their lunar spacewalk in Building 9 in April 1969. The Space Vehicle Mockup Facility in Building 9 in 2026 NASA/Robert Markowitz Apollo 13 astronaut Fred Haise trains for his lunar spacewalk in Building 29 using the six-degrees of freedom simulator in January 1970. In the Space Vehicle Mockup Facility in Building 9 in 2026, NASA astronaut Nicole Mann evaluates a new spacesuit design using the Active Response Gravity Offload System, or ARGOS. NASA/David DeHoyos Mission Simulation and Training Facility (Building 5) Construction of Building 5 , the Mission Simulation and Training Facility completed inApril 1965 and began supporting missions beginning with Gemini IV in June 1965. The building originally contained the Gemini spacecraft simulator and a Gemini translation and docking simulator. item.title: Trump promised 'no more wars'. His foreign policy tells another story
item.description: Donald Trump promised an “America First” foreign policy and pledged to keep the US out of foreign wars. From the war in Ukraine and threats to Greenland and Canada, to the US intervention in Venezuela, Trump's shifting approach to the Middle East and war with Iran, Vedika Bahl examines his foreign policy record since returning to office.

item.title: Third person dies of bird flu since virus started jumping to livestock
item.description: A person in Washington state has died from bird flu after exposure at an infected dairy farm, state health officials reported Sunday . It marks the third human bird flu death in the US since a strain of highly pathogenic (H5) avian influenza (HPAI) made the unprecedented jump from wild, migratory birds to dairy cows, which was first reported in the US in March 2024 . The person who died was a Yakima County resident and was said to have had underlying health conditions, which could have made the person more vulnerable to the infection. On Friday, county officials reported that the person was severely ill and hospitalized . In the subsequent announcement of the person's death, officials said they would not be releasing further information about the person, including their name, gender, or age, out of respect for the family's privacy. "Our hearts go out to the individual's family and loved ones during this difficult time," Dave Atteberry, health officer for the Yakima Health District, said in a statement. "Avian influenza can cause severe illness, particularly among people who have underlying health conditions. While this is a serious and heartbreaking outcome, the risk to the general public remains low." Read full article Comments

item.title: AI could break legal systems by finding previously hidden loopholes
item.description: If AI can find the holes in programming code, it can do the same with legal code, paving the way for chaos. Felix Ringe, a visiting fellow at Stanford Law School’s liftlab and legal scholar, suggests large language models (LLMs) have become potent enough that they could break legal systems by identifying exploitable inconsistencies at scale. "Legal systems encode the foundations of social order in natural language," Ringe and collaborator Linus Folkerts argued in a blog post last week. "Similar to computer systems, the written law can contain vulnerabilities that invite exploitation." Ringe contends that while courts tend to pave over these text vulnerabilities through statutory interpretation, the ability to discover adversarially useful inconsistencies in the law in an automated way risks overwhelming the legal system's ability to bridge the gaps. To buttress his thesis, he points to recent work by other legal scholars that frames laws as vulnerable code, such as " Legal Zero-Days : A Novel Risk Vector for Advanced AI Systems" and " Hardware and Software Bugs in the Legal System " [PDF]. The analogy dates back at least to 1999, with Lawrence Lessig's Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace [PDF] and Code Is Law: On Liberty in Cyberspace . Lessig credits William J. Mitchell, in City of Bits: Space, Place, and the Infobahn (1995), with the idea that code is cyberspace's law, adding that he "drew the metaphor from others as well." Ringe has turned this on its head by proposing that law is code. The analogy between programming code and legal code works reasonably well, up to a point. Law and code both have their share of formatting pedantry and ritual. The mapping breaks down when courts get cast as a runtime environment – non-deterministic trial outcomes don't work for production applications. Discontinuities aside, Ringe's point is that AI models can surface statutory gaps at a scale that may bring the chaos currently seen in the software security ecosystem to the legal world. To demonstrate that, Ringe and Folkerts cite several potential gaps in German law that they uncovered with the help of LLMs, noting that they're only sharing legal exploits they believe could not cause serious harm. For example, an amendment to Germany's Occupational Diseases Regulation (BKV) is subject to a constitutional requirement to cite its statutory authority. But Ringe and Folkerts argue that the amendment omits a required reference. So, in theory, a journalist could request an unpublished statement submitted to Germany's occupational-diseases advisory council under freedom of information rules, challenging a confidentiality provision that the researchers argue may be invalid. Another example cited describes a transit visa rule that may be invalid because the government failed to identify the authority under which the rule was made. "We believe that with cheap legal reasoning proliferating, AI systems could jeopardize the functioning of today’s legal systems," they wrote.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Claburn
item.content:encoded: If AI can find the holes in programming code, it can do the same with legal code, paving the way for chaos. Felix Ringe, a visiting fellow at Stanford Law School’s liftlab and legal scholar, suggests large language models (LLMs) have become potent enough that they could break legal systems by identifying exploitable inconsistencies at scale. "Legal systems encode the foundations of social order in natural language," Ringe and collaborator Linus Folkerts argued in a blog post last week. "Similar to computer systems, the written law can contain vulnerabilities that invite exploitation." Ringe contends that while courts tend to pave over these text vulnerabilities through statutory interpretation, the ability to discover adversarially useful inconsistencies in the law in an automated way risks overwhelming the legal system's ability to bridge the gaps. To buttress his thesis, he points to recent work by other legal scholars that frames laws as vulnerable code, such as " Legal Zero-Days : A Novel Risk Vector for Advanced AI Systems" and " Hardware and Software Bugs in the Legal System " [PDF]. The analogy dates back at least to 1999, with Lawrence Lessig's Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace [PDF] and Code Is Law: On Liberty in Cyberspace . Lessig credits William J. Mitchell, in City of Bits: Space, Place, and the Infobahn (1995), with the idea that code is cyberspace's law, adding that he "drew the metaphor from others as well." Ringe has turned this on its head by proposing that law is code. The analogy between programming code and legal code works reasonably well, up to a point. Law and code both have their share of formatting pedantry and ritual. The mapping breaks down when courts get cast as a runtime environment – non-deterministic trial outcomes don't work for production applications. Discontinuities aside, Ringe's point is that AI models can surface statutory gaps at a scale that may bring the chaos currently seen in the software security ecosystem to the legal world. To demonstrate that, Ringe and Folkerts cite several potential gaps in German law that they uncovered with the help of LLMs, noting that they're only sharing legal exploits they believe could not cause serious harm. For example, an amendment to Germany's Occupational Diseases Regulation (BKV) is subject to a constitutional requirement to cite its statutory authority. But Ringe and Folkerts argue that the amendment omits a required reference. So, in theory, a journalist could request an unpublished statement submitted to Germany's occupational-diseases advisory council under freedom of information rules, challenging a confidentiality provision that the researchers argue may be invalid. Another example cited describes a transit visa rule that may be invalid because the government failed to identify the authority under which the rule was made. "We believe that with cheap legal reasoning proliferating, AI systems could jeopardize the functioning of today’s legal systems," they wrote. "In such a world, lawmakers would need to significantly harden the process of legislation, for example by leveraging advanced AI themselves." Wendy Musell, a San Francisco-based employment law attorney and partner, told The Register that the use of AI in the legal field is expanding rapidly. "Some California Courts, including LA Superior Court, are testing the use of AI as law clerks," said Musell. "Generally law clerks would assist the Court by researching and drafting opinions for the judge's review. That means AI is serving that role in certain courts. Litigators now must consider how AI is analyzing motions and cases. "This is the case even where I personally have found different AI sources to appear to have a slant or bias, and often fail to accurately analyze legal issues. It was just a matter of time before AI came for the legislative process." Eric Goldman, associate dean for research and professor of law at Santa Clara University School of Law, told The Register that Ringe's argument has some merit. "I think the methodology of using AI to identify potential statutory gaps is logical," said Goldman. "However, it will require careful human review to determine if the AI-identified gaps are in fact actually gaps. Statutory gaps also may have no legal consequence, or at least none of significance; and legislatures will often correct any major gaps once they are identified." Goldman said the idea that legislators should use AI during the drafting process is ambitious, at least in the short term. "Legislators often draft laws with a range of goals and priorities, and avoiding statutory gaps is rarely a high priority," he explained. "But many legislatures have legislative counsel who are responsible for converting draft bills into final legislative text, and I could see where legislative counsel could benefit from using AI to identify drafting gaps as part of their standard cleanup protocols." ®

item.title: The Long Hull: Karl Bushby reflects on perseverance & 'best of humanity' on his 28-year journey home
item.description: "They say it takes a village. In this case, it took a world." After 28 years and some 50,000 kilometres, British explorer and adventurer Karl Bushby has returned to his hometown of Hull, completing an extraordinary life journey across four continents that illustrates not only the limits of human endurance, but also the intricate relationship between individual determination, geopolitical constraints and a world of humanity.

item.title: TB 26-09 Measured Hammer-Tap Inputs
item.description: For more information, contact Joel W. Sills, Langley Research Center, joel.w.sills@nasa.gov . Download the PDF version An instrumented hammer test does not require an idealized single half-sine waveform. When the complete force and response are measured accurately, crest ripples and separated contacts remain known inputs. Force shape changes excitation, but does not inherently invalidate the record. Adequacy depends on measurement accuracy, bandwidth, signal-to-noise ratio, and coverage of the test objective. Background: What the Hammer Actually Measures Hammer tests support modal analysis [2–4] and can precede pyroshock testing [6]. Figure 1 compares a half-sine, maintained-contact rippling, and separated contacts. During a zero-force interval, the structure continues to vibrate; re-contact acts on that vibration. If an exact model and test article receive the same force and initial conditions, uniqueness gives identical responses for each bounded measured history. An approximate model can show different errors as inputs excite different frequencies, amplitudes, or nonlinear states. See [1] for the exact-model derivation. Analysis: A Half-Sine Is Broadband, but Not Flat Figure 2 shows that a finite half-sine is broadband but contains spectral zeros at f/fo = 3, 5, 7, …, with fo = 1/(2T) for pulse duration T. Its appearance alone cannot establish adequate excitation. Analysis: Spectral Content Is Determined by the Measured Force History Figure 3 normalizes each spectrum to its own DC value. Crest rippling adds content and can fill half-sine notches. Timing between separated contacts creates deterministic interference. For adequacy, inspect the unnormalized measured spectrum and response signal-to-noise ratio. Recommended Practice: Evaluate Test Adequacy Against the Intended Objective • Measure the complete applied force with adequate bandwidth, calibration, dynamic range, and time synchronization. • Verify that the response measurements have adequate bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio and are not clipped or saturated. • Confirm that the excitation covers the frequency, amplitude, and nonlinear-response ranges required by the intended test objective. • Reject or repeat a test only for an identified measurement, excitation, or coverage deficiency. Conclusion Half-sine appearance neither establishes validity nor guarantees adequacy. Judge each hammer test by its purpose and by accurate, complete force and response measurements over the required range. References 1. A. Majed, J. Sills, E. Henkel, V. Babuska, S. Yunis, D. Hamilton, J. Akers, and T. Kinney, Validity and Predictability of Measured Hammer Tap Inputs: Linear and Nonlinear Structural Systems, September 2026. 2. D. J. Ewins, Modal Testing: Theory, Practice and Application, 2nd ed., 2000. 3. ISO 7626-5:2019, Mechanical Vibration and Shock—Experimental Determination of Mechanical Mobility—Part 5 4. K. G. McConnell and P. S. Varoto, Vibration Testing: Theory and Practice, 2nd ed., 2008. 5. A.

item.title: One of Google’s Android partners turned 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet
item.description: A current Videostrong Android TV device. Google says one of its Android manufacturing partners secretly built a backdoor in 1.3 million devices and turned them into a botnet. The company says it has now dismantled the backdoor and "cut ties" with the manufacturer, the Shenzhen, China-based Videostrong Technology Co., which has been banned from building or selling certified Android devices or supplying software for them. The infected devices were used without owners' knowledge for "malicious activity," like ad fraud, data exfiltration, and routing unauthorized network traffic. Google claims the "backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial … Read the full story at The Verge.

item.title: EU says fridge attacks 'deliberate attempt to disrupt' bloc's food supply
item.description: Grocery stores from Sweden to Portugal were hit Monday by a suspected cyberattack on their freezer systems, in what the EU denounced as a deliberate attempt to disrupt the bloc's food chain. Supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg and the Netherlands were among at least eight countries affected in the incident, which came three weeks after a cyberattack caused mass disruption in French grocery stores. Food retailers were forced to throw out produce that had spoiled or was at risk of spoiling after refrigerator temperatures soared overnight. FRANCE 24's Dave Keating reports from Brussels.

item.title: BMW is taking on Tesla’s FSD with urban driver assist starting in 2027
item.description: BMW says that it will expand its navigation-guided, partially automated driving capabilities into urban environments starting in 2027, launching first in Germany with other markets to follow. The new system can help steer, speed up, and slow down the vehicle on both highways and city streets using its built-in GPS navigation. While driving in town, it can assist with changing lanes, making turns, yielding to other cars, and driving through roundabouts. But as a Level 2 driver assist system, it still requires drivers to keep their eyes on the road and stay ready to take over at any moment. item.title: Revisiting the Superclásico: a story of death, violence, colour and family
item.description: Attending Boca v River in the week I turned 60 made me recall a lifetime of experiences at the fixture Ever since the Observer Sport Monthly published a list of 50 sporting things you must do before you die with Watch Boca Juniors Play River Plate in Buenos Aires at No 1 in 2004, the biggest super derby in Argentina has been firmly positioned in the global imagination; its reputation for colour, passion and uncontainable emotion acquiring an almost glamorous sheen. The thump and thud of the coordinated chants, the shiny ticker-tape amid flare smoke matching the teams’ strips, the bounce of the concrete as tens of thousands jump in unison, mounted police surrounding the stadium, avalanche stoppers set alight, rockets aimed at players; blood and fire. Exciting, right? Continue reading...

item.title: Dinosaur red blood cells recovered from 115-million-year-old fossil
item.description: Illustration of the Aratasaurus museunacionali dinosaur whose fossils contained red blood cells Victor O. Leshyk A nondescript 115-million-year-old fragment of leg bone has yielded spectacularly preserved red blood cells, which may be the earliest ever found in dinosaurs. Red blood cells have previously been found in dinosaur remains, including 75-million-year-old bone fragments collected in Canada in 2015 and the femur of a Tyrannosaurus rex that died 68 million years ago , found in Montana in 2005. Read more Exquisite 66-million-year-old bird feather preserved in dinosaur dropping Now, Kliti Grice at Curtin University in Perth, Australia, and her colleagues say they have isolated the oldest-ever dinosaur red blood cells from the hind-limb of a theropod dinosaur, Aratasaurus museunacionali , found in Brazil in 2008. Advertisement The Aratasaurus individual studied by the team wasn’t yet fully grown, with an estimated body length of just over 3 metres, and weighed about 34 kilograms. “The fossils we worked on are not display specimens by any means, so they don’t look very interesting,” says Grice. “If you look at them, you think there’s just a bunch of bones and there’s probably not much in there.” A dinosaur bone fragment containing fossilised red blood cells Curtin University However, when she etched out part of the fossils, using hydrochloric acid to dissolve surrounding rock, she was shocked at what she saw. “I was jumping up and down,” says Grice. “I ran up to my head of school’s office and was so excited that he gave me a whisky to calm me down. No one has ever seen dinosaur red blood cells in high resolution before.” The cells she found were abundant: in a single slide, just a fifth of a millimetre wide, there were 20 blood cells. All of the cells were within fossilised blood vessels, providing further evidence that they really were red blood cells. Liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry analysis revealed the presence of haem B, a constituent of haemoglobin that binds to oxygen, adding molecular evidence of the type of cell. The team also had to rule out the possibility of any contamination, especially from the sediments in which the fossil was preserved, which were dominated by algae. Microscopic images of structures resembling red blood cells from the fossilised limb bone of Aratasaurus museunacionali Curtin University The cells found outside the bone were dominated by chlorophyll-derived compounds, whereas those inside contained haem-derived molecules, which strongly suggests that the latter cells weren’t a result of contamination. The researchers also compared the blood cells to those of the closest living relatives of the dinosaur fossil, birds and crocodiles. The Aratasaurus red blood cells are significantly larger. This could indicate that the cells swelled during fossilisation, or that the species grew much bigger than the fossilised specimen. item.content:encoded: Illustration of the Aratasaurus museunacionali dinosaur whose fossils contained red blood cells Victor O. Leshyk A nondescript 115-million-year-old fragment of leg bone has yielded spectacularly preserved red blood cells, which may be the earliest ever found in dinosaurs. Red blood cells have previously been found in dinosaur remains, including 75-million-year-old bone fragments collected in Canada in 2015 and the femur of a Tyrannosaurus rex that died 68 million years ago , found in Montana in 2005. Read more Exquisite 66-million-year-old bird feather preserved in dinosaur dropping Now, Kliti Grice at Curtin University in Perth, Australia, and her colleagues say they have isolated the oldest-ever dinosaur red blood cells from the hind-limb of a theropod dinosaur, Aratasaurus museunacionali , found in Brazil in 2008. Advertisement The Aratasaurus individual studied by the team wasn’t yet fully grown, with an estimated body length of just over 3 metres, and weighed about 34 kilograms. “The fossils we worked on are not display specimens by any means, so they don’t look very interesting,” says Grice. “If you look at them, you think there’s just a bunch of bones and there’s probably not much in there.” A dinosaur bone fragment containing fossilised red blood cells Curtin University However, when she etched out part of the fossils, using hydrochloric acid to dissolve surrounding rock, she was shocked at what she saw. “I was jumping up and down,” says Grice. “I ran up to my head of school’s office and was so excited that he gave me a whisky to calm me down. No one has ever seen dinosaur red blood cells in high resolution before.” The cells she found were abundant: in a single slide, just a fifth of a millimetre wide, there were 20 blood cells. All of the cells were within fossilised blood vessels, providing further evidence that they really were red blood cells. Liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry analysis revealed the presence of haem B, a constituent of haemoglobin that binds to oxygen, adding molecular evidence of the type of cell. The team also had to rule out the possibility of any contamination, especially from the sediments in which the fossil was preserved, which were dominated by algae. Microscopic images of structures resembling red blood cells from the fossilised limb bone of Aratasaurus museunacionali Curtin University The cells found outside the bone were dominated by chlorophyll-derived compounds, whereas those inside contained haem-derived molecules, which strongly suggests that the latter cells weren’t a result of contamination. The researchers also compared the blood cells to those of the closest living relatives of the dinosaur fossil, birds and crocodiles. The Aratasaurus red blood cells are significantly larger. This could indicate that the cells swelled during fossilisation, or that the species grew much bigger than the fossilised specimen. Grice says the discovery may mean that other nondescript dinosaur fossils that have been locked away in museum collections may hold profound secrets. “There’s drawers and drawers of fossil material, which don’t look very nice,” she says. “This kind of work opens up a whole new opportunity to unlock those collections and bring modern technology and molecular techniques to these specimens.” Journal reference: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2614248123

item.title: Zapping part of the brain makes you think harder – at a cost
item.description: Exhausted after a day of thinking? Brain zapping could help, temporarily bookzv/Shutterstock Struggling with a difficult mental task? Zapping the brain region linked to our motivation to make a mental effort might help – for a while. People who had this part of their brain stimulated by electrical currents excelled at a difficult task, but also became more mentally fatigued afterwards. “Their performance is much better; however, this good performance comes with lower motivation in the end,” says Hongmei Xia at the University of Munich, Germany. Read more Your brain’s unexpected ability to regenerate and how to harness it Xia and her colleagues put electrodes on the heads of 31 volunteers with no known health conditions. During a half-hour session in an MRI scanner, the volunteers spent 20 minutes doing the 3-back memory test, where you have to remember and identify the third item back as an ongoing sequence is presented to you – a very demanding mental task. They were then offered €1 for doing an easy test or €2 for a harder one. Advertisement During the 3-back memory test, the electrodes delivered transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) to a region of the brain called the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex to randomly chosen volunteers, who were unaware they were receiving it. Other studies have shown the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is involved in controlling the cognitive effort we make. “Our dorsolateral prefrontal cortex helps us to work hard,” says Xia. The volunteers who had tDCS reacted faster and more accurately than those who didn’t receive this stimulation. For instance, their average reaction time was 0.98 seconds, compared with 1.12 seconds with sham stimulation. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter Xia thinks stimulating the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex will boost brain performance generally. “I can imagine any cognitive task will be better, but afterwards you will feel more fatigued,” she says. After the tests, the volunteers who got tDCS had higher levels of the neurotransmitter glutamate in their dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, according to a non-invasive technique called magnetic resonance spectroscopy. The higher their glutamate levels, the more likely they were to choose the €1 task over the €2 one. Some researchers think mental fatigue is a result of the buildup of glutamate , which can harm cells at high levels. Xia thinks her team’s findings are the strongest evidence of this yet. The findings suggest it is important to take a break when you feel mentally tired, she says. Xia thinks future studies should also look at the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in people with conditions such as depression, which can affect motivation. item.dc:creator: Michael Le Page
item.content:encoded: Exhausted after a day of thinking? Brain zapping could help, temporarily bookzv/Shutterstock Struggling with a difficult mental task? Zapping the brain region linked to our motivation to make a mental effort might help – for a while. People who had this part of their brain stimulated by electrical currents excelled at a difficult task, but also became more mentally fatigued afterwards. “Their performance is much better; however, this good performance comes with lower motivation in the end,” says Hongmei Xia at the University of Munich, Germany. Read more Your brain’s unexpected ability to regenerate and how to harness it Xia and her colleagues put electrodes on the heads of 31 volunteers with no known health conditions. During a half-hour session in an MRI scanner, the volunteers spent 20 minutes doing the 3-back memory test, where you have to remember and identify the third item back as an ongoing sequence is presented to you – a very demanding mental task. They were then offered €1 for doing an easy test or €2 for a harder one. Advertisement During the 3-back memory test, the electrodes delivered transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) to a region of the brain called the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex to randomly chosen volunteers, who were unaware they were receiving it. Other studies have shown the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is involved in controlling the cognitive effort we make. “Our dorsolateral prefrontal cortex helps us to work hard,” says Xia. The volunteers who had tDCS reacted faster and more accurately than those who didn’t receive this stimulation. For instance, their average reaction time was 0.98 seconds, compared with 1.12 seconds with sham stimulation. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter Xia thinks stimulating the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex will boost brain performance generally. “I can imagine any cognitive task will be better, but afterwards you will feel more fatigued,” she says. After the tests, the volunteers who got tDCS had higher levels of the neurotransmitter glutamate in their dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, according to a non-invasive technique called magnetic resonance spectroscopy. The higher their glutamate levels, the more likely they were to choose the €1 task over the €2 one. Some researchers think mental fatigue is a result of the buildup of glutamate , which can harm cells at high levels. Xia thinks her team’s findings are the strongest evidence of this yet. The findings suggest it is important to take a break when you feel mentally tired, she says. Xia thinks future studies should also look at the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in people with conditions such as depression, which can affect motivation. Curiosity may be what drives our brains to become so complex We often think that our ability to be curious stems from our complex, human brain – but what if curiosity shapes that complexity? “I think the claim that the stimulation made people ‘work harder’ is well substantiated,” says neuroscientist Emile Radyte at Samphire Neuroscience, a UK-based company exploring the use of tDCS to treat conditions such as premenstrual syndrome. But the study doesn’t prove that higher glutamate levels were the cause of the greater mental fatigue, she says. Radyte says her trials have shown that if productivity is hindered by conditions such as premenstrual syndrome, applying tDCS over the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex can restore it. But she isn’t sure about using it to boost mental performance. “A 20-minute laboratory task does not establish a net productivity benefit over a working day,” says Radyte. It is a good study, says Nilli Lavie at University College London, but the greater mental fatigue could be a result of using more neural energy , rather than the buildup of glutamate. It’s also hard to precisely target the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex with tDCS without an MRI scanner to guide you, says Lavie. “Drink coffee instead,” she says. Journal Reference: PNAS DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2534136123

item.title: New 'Star Trek: The Original Voyages' book traces the stellar legacy of the bold sci-fi brand
item.description: null "Star Trek" celebrated its diamond anniversary last month, marking 60 years since it first aired on NBC on Sept. 8, 1966. There were a bunch of Trekkie-themed celebrations and news stories over September, including festive documentaries , special screenings , tributes, parade floats , interviews, and even a Galileo shuttle story. Now, publishers Penguin Random House and Ten Speed Press are releasing " Star Trek: The Original Voyages: A Visual History " on Nov. 10, 2026. This coffee table book promises unprecedented exploration of the pioneering space fantasy television series and enduring pop culture property that bolstered the space race and ignited sci-fi audiences' imaginations by taking us to strange new worlds and civilizations in the final frontier. It's a striking 416-page hardback written by Kyle Newman and Jeff Bond, documenting all the classic characters and plotlines that are still inspiring artists, filmmakers, authors, and astronauts around the globe six decades later, and we’ve got our hands on a primo copy to show off. "When the original 'Star Trek' series burst onto the screen in 1966, few could have anticipated the enduring legacy it would create," states the synopsis. "Although it lasted just three seasons and 79 episodes, 'Star Trek' left an indelible mark on popular culture, and it soon spawned an animated television series, a blockbuster major motion picture franchise, and for its most dedicated fans, a way of life. "Star Trek: The Original Voyages" is a fantastic tribute to the iconic brand Penguin Random House The vivid back cover of "Star Trek: The Original Voyages," coming Nov. 10. Penguin Random House "The story of the U.S.S. Enterprise and her crew—James T. Kirk (William Shatner), Spock (Leonard Nimoy), Leonard McCoy (DeForest Kelley), Montgomery Scott (James Doohan), Nyota Uhura (Nichelle Nichols), Pavel Chekov (Walter Koenig), and Hikaru Sulu (George Takei)—as well as the behind-the-scenes story of its creators, The Great Bird of the Galaxy Gene Roddenberry and his many collaborators, is extraordinary." Inside this classy collector's edition, which is the first volume of a two-book series gazing back at the complete history of "Star Trek," readers will behold a wealth of archival photos, costumes, storyboards, cast and creators' chats, behind-the-scenes ephemera, props, and filming models. A page from "Star Trek: The Original Voyages," coming Nov. 10. Penguin Random House A page from "Star Trek: The Original Voyages," coming Nov. 10. Penguin Random House "Star Trek: The Original Voyages" chronicles not just the iconic TV show but also the short-lived animated series and all six of the big-screen "Star Trek" feature films up to the year 1991. Above and beyond the dramatic cover emblazoned with reflective lettering, this beefy "Trek" book truly leaps into warp speed, covering all the licensed toys, comic books, convention memorabilia, media parodies, promotional roadshows, trading cards, and vintage magazine covers
item.dc:creator: Jeff Spry
item.content:encoded: null "Star Trek" celebrated its diamond anniversary last month, marking 60 years since it first aired on NBC on Sept. 8, 1966. There were a bunch of Trekkie-themed celebrations and news stories over September, including festive documentaries , special screenings , tributes, parade floats , interviews, and even a Galileo shuttle story. Now, publishers Penguin Random House and Ten Speed Press are releasing " Star Trek: The Original Voyages: A Visual History " on Nov. 10, 2026. This coffee table book promises unprecedented exploration of the pioneering space fantasy television series and enduring pop culture property that bolstered the space race and ignited sci-fi audiences' imaginations by taking us to strange new worlds and civilizations in the final frontier. It's a striking 416-page hardback written by Kyle Newman and Jeff Bond, documenting all the classic characters and plotlines that are still inspiring artists, filmmakers, authors, and astronauts around the globe six decades later, and we’ve got our hands on a primo copy to show off. "When the original 'Star Trek' series burst onto the screen in 1966, few could have anticipated the enduring legacy it would create," states the synopsis. "Although it lasted just three seasons and 79 episodes, 'Star Trek' left an indelible mark on popular culture, and it soon spawned an animated television series, a blockbuster major motion picture franchise, and for its most dedicated fans, a way of life. "Star Trek: The Original Voyages" is a fantastic tribute to the iconic brand Penguin Random House The vivid back cover of "Star Trek: The Original Voyages," coming Nov. 10. Penguin Random House "The story of the U.S.S. Enterprise and her crew—James T. Kirk (William Shatner), Spock (Leonard Nimoy), Leonard McCoy (DeForest Kelley), Montgomery Scott (James Doohan), Nyota Uhura (Nichelle Nichols), Pavel Chekov (Walter Koenig), and Hikaru Sulu (George Takei)—as well as the behind-the-scenes story of its creators, The Great Bird of the Galaxy Gene Roddenberry and his many collaborators, is extraordinary." Inside this classy collector's edition, which is the first volume of a two-book series gazing back at the complete history of "Star Trek," readers will behold a wealth of archival photos, costumes, storyboards, cast and creators' chats, behind-the-scenes ephemera, props, and filming models. A page from "Star Trek: The Original Voyages," coming Nov. 10. Penguin Random House A page from "Star Trek: The Original Voyages," coming Nov. 10. Penguin Random House "Star Trek: The Original Voyages" chronicles not just the iconic TV show but also the short-lived animated series and all six of the big-screen "Star Trek" feature films up to the year 1991. Above and beyond the dramatic cover emblazoned with reflective lettering, this beefy "Trek" book truly leaps into warp speed, covering all the licensed toys, comic books, convention memorabilia, media parodies, promotional roadshows, trading cards, and vintage magazine covers. "Star Trek: The Original Voyages: A Visual History" lands on Nov. 10, 2026. Star Trek: The Original Voyages: A Visual History: $60 Boldly celebrate 60 years of Star Trek with this official visual history of the original series, documenting how its iconic characters and storylines reshaped the science fiction genre. item.title: Googling "Zelda" today offers a glimpse of how search worked in 1998
item.description: The year was 1998. Britney Spears topped the charts, Bill Clinton was impeached, and a couple of little websites called Google and Ars Technica came online. It was also the year Nintendo released The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on the Nintendo 64. Google, which has come to dominate the Internet (Ars is still working on that), is celebrating the imminent release of the Ocarina of Time remaster by temporarily transporting us back to that storied year with a search Easter egg. To access the Google time machine, you just have to search for either "Zelda" or "Ocarina of Time." Google will load the standard 2026 results page, but you'll see an animated Master Sword in the lower right corner. It appears on both mobile and desktop—just click the sword and enjoy the show. After a little time-skipping animation and a Link shout (you know the one), you'll swear it's 1998 again. The search page is transformed into a simple list of blue links with retro Google branding. This is particularly apt given the time-shifting mechanics in Ocarina of Time . Read full article Comments

item.title: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is $100 off, matching its best price to date
item.description: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the company’s most capable smartwatch. Whether you intend to put its many tracking features to the test, or you simply want the longest battery life of any Apple Watch, it’s currently on sale for $699.99 ($100 off) in multiple colors at Amazon , matching its all-time low price. Apple Watch Ultra 4 Where to Buy: $799 $699 at Amazon Powered by Apple’s new S11 chip (also in the Series 12), the Apple Watch Ultra 4 delivers faster performance than the last-gen version, plus a handful of new Apple Intelligence features. Of note, those include Sound Recognition, which alerts you to noises like alarms and doorbells, and the Live Rewind feature that lets you revisit the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation. An upcoming Siri Recap feature will be able to create summaries of conversations for later reference. This model has broader health and fitness capabilities than previous models, too. Its sensors promise more accurate EKG measurements, while the watch can track your heart rate as often as every five seconds. The new Readiness feature (not available on the Ultra 3 and earlier models) also analyzes your recent activity, sleep quality, and other health metrics to generate a score from zero to 10, helping you determine whether to push yourself or take it easy. On the hardware front, battery life is perhaps the biggest highlight, with Apple promising up to 50 hours on a charge — twice as long as the Series 12 . Like its predecessor, this model features Apple’s brightest watch display and a rugged design that’s water-resistant up to 100 meters and IP6X-rated for dust resistance. It also retains conveniences like the second-generation Ultra Wideband chip for Precision Finding, and helpful gesture controls so you can you can perform actions with a double tap or flick of your wrist. Read our hands-on impressions of the Apple Watch Ultra 4. Three more ways to save Ugreen’s FineTrack2 Bluetooth tracker is on sale for $13.99 at Amazon , just a few cents shy of its best price to date. The soccer ball-shaped tracker stands out with its playful design, but it also offers some useful features including a non-rechargeable battery can last up to seven years. It works with Apple’s expansive Find My network to help you locate misplaced belongings, while its lanyard makes it easy to attach to your keys, bag, or other items. If you’re looking to spruce up your Apple Watch Ultra or Series smartwatch, a variety of Apple’s official bands are on sale for up to 69 percent off at Woot . The silicone Sport Band is down to $14.99 ($35 off) , while the soft, breathable Sport Loop is available for $19.99 ($29 off) . You can also grab the rugged Trail Loop for $34.99 ($64 off) . Hoto’s new Pulse 4-in-1 Cordless Staple Gun is on sale for $69.99 ($10 off) at Amazon . The versatile tool can help with repairing stuff, or putting together decorations. item.title: MAGA: Why are Trump's most loyal supporters turning against him?
item.description: Is Trump losing the support of the very coalition that brought him back to power? Just one day before the midterm elections, Trump's approval rating stands at 32%, one of the lowest ever recorded at this stage of a presidency. And discontent is growing beyond Democratic voters. Some of Trump's most loyal Republican and MAGA supporters are increasingly torn between political loyalty and economic reality. The war in Iran, rising costs linked to the Strait of Hormuz blockade, unfulfilled “America First” promises and other controversial issues, including the Epstein files scandal, are widening the rift between Trump and his electoral base. Can he regain control of the diverse coalition that makes up MAGA? FRANCE 24 journalist Stella Elgersma spoke to MAGA and Republican experts to explore how the movement has evolved, what its supporters want and what is driving their discontent. Watch the full youtube documentary : https://youtu.be/XkehRG77itY?si=iOfIl0PwrgyX-j0X

item.title: Israeli 'unity government': Efrat Shapira expects Herzog will urge rival camps to form a 'coalition'
item.description: Erin Ogunkeye is pleased to welcome Efrat Shapira Rosenberg, Israeli Radio/TV Host, Columnist, Podcaster and Educator. Following a deadlocked Israeli election, “everyone is saying who they’re not going to sit with, but no one is actually saying who they will sit with.” As President Isaac Herzog prepares to consult parliamentary factions over the formation of a new coalition, the impasse reveals tensions that extend beyond the familiar confrontation between Benjamin Netanyahu and his political opponents. According to Shapira, co-host of the highly popular Israeli politics podcast Miflaget Hamakshavot, the divisions are equally pronounced within the opposition bloc supporting Gadi Eisenkot.

item.title: Most of our measures of a key cognitive process don't agree
item.description: It's widely acknowledged that it's nearly impossible to publish negative results in scientific journals. "We didn't see anything" is a much harder sell than finding that a hypothesis is clearly right. Findings of no effect tend to either be shuffled off to low-profile journals or left behind as unpublished lab lore. The high-profile journal Nature, however, made a notable exception this week, publishing a study that tells us that a bunch of methods we have been using to try to measure a key emotional ability don't seem to be measuring the same thing. The results mean that we don't have a good way to measure the impact of a concept that is the basis of a key method in therapy. Inconsistencies One of the most successful forms of therapy is cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT. In part, CBT is based on getting people to step back and engage in "cognitive reappraisal." This requires people to think over a situation that has caused a negative emotional response and find ways to reinterpret it so that it has less impact on them. The ability to engage in this process has been linked to emotional resilience. Read full article Comments

item.title: Cops bust botnet of 1.3M infected Android TV boxes
item.description: A coalition of private-sector security firms working with Japan’s National Police Agency has disrupted XCPE, a backdoor used to build a massive botnet comprising more than 1.3 million Android devices across more than 200 countries. Google, Lumen, Human Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI participated in the disruption. “We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology,” the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a Monday blog. Videostrong Technology is a hardware manufacturer based in Shenzhen, China. It builds Android devices, including home TV boxes and projectors. According to Google, Videostrong deliberately embedded the XCPE backdoor in device firmware and sold access to criminal affiliates , allowing them to install additional malware modules on devices shipped to unsuspecting customers. When buyers connected these devices to their home networks, the preinstalled backdoor allowed operators to create proxy networks and hide malicious traffic using the customers' internet connections without their knowledge. The firmware’s pre-installed management agent purported to be a standard remote-management client, according to TrendAI. It pulled updates from a GitHub page, and connected to a Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) server that gave the operator full remote control of each box, allowing them to install and remove apps, change settings, and push updates to the infected devices. Between June 3 and October 1, TrendAI documented more than 3.8 million distinct home and mobile IP addresses connected to the operation. The coalition also disrupted the command-and-control domains used to manage the affiliate modules. “Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices,” according to GTIG. Google said it had since cut ties with Videostrong, and banned the OEM from making devices with preloaded Google apps. Videostrong did not immediately respond to The Register’ s inquiries. This backdoor and botnet operation is part of the same ecosystem as BadBox 2.0 , another notorious botnet that infected more than 10 million TV boxes and other devices before Human, Google, and TrendAI disrupted it in March 2025.®

item.title: Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II EVO FE (APO) lens review — how good is this budget lens for astrophotography?
item.description: null Key specs Type: Full-frame prime lens Focal length: 35 mm Maximum aperture: f/1.8 Lens mount: Sony FE & Nikon Z Weight: 12.52 oz / 355 g Dimensions: 3.33 x 4.37 in / 69 x 76 mm Filter thread: 58 mm Release date: April 2026 Budget primes can be, surprisingly, excellent choices for photographers shooting all subjects. It’s all too easy to get carried away with the best specs, such as a large maximum aperture and impressive optical design often seen in more expensive options. But affordable lenses like the Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II FE (APO) have the potential to impress and delight in equal measure. The 35mm f/1.8 is a compact and lightweight lens offering a reasonably fast maximum aperture, making it a prime candidate for astrophotography. It’s also the same size and almost the same weight as the Viltrox AF 55mm f/1.8 FE (APO), another lens that could potentially grace your camera bag. With a highly attractive price tag of just $399 / £385, and mount options for Nikon Z and Sony FE, many astrophotographers will be wondering if this is a lens worth considering. It features 13 elements in 10 groups, as well as featuring an apochromatic (APO) design for reducing chromatic aberration as much as possible. As much as possible is key here because not all lenses are as successful as the manufacturer claims, although that’s not a comment on the 35mm f/1.8. Read on to discover if this could be one of the best lenses for astrophotography . Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II EVO FE (APO) lens review Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II EVO FE (APO): Performance The Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 FE (APO) balances well with Sony A series cameras. (Image credit: James Abbott) Sharp images for the price Sweet spot at f/8-f/11, not ideal for astro Some astigmatism at the edges of the frame For a budget lens, the 35mm f/1.8 produces great, yet not perfect, image quality. On the plus side, images are nice and sharp, particularly in the centre, even when shooting wide open at f/1.8. At this aperture setting, though, there is some astigmatism at the left edges of the frame. This is where stars appear as crosses. This is a surprise since it’s an APO lens, and, equally surprising, it’s isolated, but it is something you have to consider. You do have to zoom into the image to see it, so it may not be a dealbreaker. Photos shot at f/1.8 are sharpest in the centre, with some fall-off towards the edges, with the corners exhibiting the least sharpness. There’s also the strongest vignetting at f/1.8. At the time of writing, there’s no Adobe Lightroom lens profile for the lens, but you can manually remove the vignetting and even create a preset of your own. Aperture f/1.8, shutter speed 5 secs, ISO 800. Shot with a Sony A7R V and a Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 FE (APO) on a Three Legged Thing PUNKS Brian 2.0 tripod. On the plus side, images are nice and sharp, particularly in the centre, even when shooting wide open at f/1.8. At this aperture setting, though, there is some astigmatism at the left edges of the frame. This is where stars appear as crosses. This is a surprise since it’s an APO lens, and, equally surprising, it’s isolated, but it is something you have to consider. You do have to zoom into the image to see it, so it may not be a dealbreaker. Photos shot at f/1.8 are sharpest in the centre, with some fall-off towards the edges, with the corners exhibiting the least sharpness. There’s also the strongest vignetting at f/1.8. At the time of writing, there’s no Adobe Lightroom lens profile for the lens, but you can manually remove the vignetting and even create a preset of your own. Aperture f/1.8, shutter speed 5 secs, ISO 800. Shot with a Sony A7R V and a Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 FE (APO) on a Three Legged Thing PUNKS Brian 2.0 tripod. James Abbott Aperture f/1.8, shutter speed 5 secs, ISO 800. Shot with a Sony A7R V and a Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 FE (APO) on a Three Legged Thing PUNKS Brian 2.0 tripod. James Abbott Aperture f/1.8, shutter speed 5 secs, ISO 800. Shot with a Sony A7R V and a Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 FE (APO) on a Three Legged Thing PUNKS Brian 2.0 tripod. James Abbott Aperture f/1.8, shutter speed 5 secs, ISO 800. Shot with a Sony A7R V and a Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 FE (APO) on a Three Legged Thing PUNKS Brian 2.0 tripod. James Abbott Aperture f/1.8, shutter speed 5 secs, ISO 800. Shot with a Sony A7R V and a Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 FE (APO) on a Three Legged Thing PUNKS Brian 2.0 tripod. James Abbott The vignette disappears as soon as f/4, with a gradual increase in sharpness across the frame between f/2.8 and f/5.6. f/8 and f/11 appear identical in terms of sharpness and occupy the sweet spot, while diffraction is clearly at work when you stop down to f/16. In reality, it’s unlikely you’d shoot beyond f/11 with this lens, even if you were shooting landscapes. Overall, image quality is impressive despite not being perfect and stopping down to f/2.8 when shooting astro does provide greater clarity across the frame. This is, as you know, at the expense of having to shoot at a slightly higher ISO setting to compensate. Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II EVO FE (APO): Design The Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 FE (APO) is compact and lightweight. (Image credit: James Abbott) Compact and lightweight Manual aperture ring Weather sealed While f/1.8 lenses may not have the speed and light-gathering capabilities of faster f/1.4 and f/1.2 lenses, they’re considerably smaller and lighter. The lens only has a 58mm filter thread, so if you use any night filters, they will be at the less expensive end of the price scale. For some photographers, the slight speed reduction of f/1.8 is a worthy compromise, and at 3.33 x 4.37 in / 69 x 76 mm with a weight of 12.52 oz / 355 g, the 35mm f/1.8 is beautifully compact and balances well with camera bodies. Build quality is excellent, and it’s fair to say the lens belies its budget price tag. The metal build alongside the manual aperture ring gives the 35mm f/1.8 a much more premium look and feel. The aperture ring can also be set to A for in-body aperture adjustments, as well as offering the ability to switch the aperture click on and off. The latter is most popular with videographers. There’s also a customizable Fn button on the side. The lens has an aperture ring that, when combined with its lustrous finish, provides a premium feel. James Abbott Stills photographers love a click on their cameras, but for video it's problematic. Hence the 'CLICK on/off' switch on the lens body. James Abbott On the other side, a focus control switch moves between autofocus and manual. James Abbott While the front element is small and not as ideal for light-gathering as larger lenses, this helps keep costs down and the 58mm filter thread means filters will also be inexpensive, to boot. James Abbott The lens is weather-sealed against light rain and dust, with a rubber gasket on the lens mount. The front element also features a water and smudge-resistant coating, which is certainly useful for outdoor photography. Plus, there’s a minimum focusing distance of just 13.4 in / 34 cm, which is useful for daylight photography but of no consequence for astrophotography. The 35mm f/1.8 is made up of 13 elements in 10 groups, and as previously mentioned, features an APO design, which is intended to eliminate chromatic aberration in high-contrast scenes. The elements include two extra-low dispersion (ED), three high refractive index (HR) and one ultra aspherical (UA). The UA lens is claimed to be Viltrox’s LAB Series quality, which matches the Viltrox flagship line-up. Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II EVO FE (APO): Functionality The Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 FE (APO) features a 58 mm filter thread, keeping filter prices on the lower side compared to larger ones. (Image credit: James Abbott) Smooth manual focus Internal focusing Stepping motor-powered AF When it comes to features, prime lenses are always pretty basic, with few features to shout about. The 35mm f/1.8 is certainly no exception, but its build quality and overall design hold up alongside its image quality and reasonably fast maximum aperture. It does, however, have a few points worth mentioning. One feature that many Viltrox lenses have, including the 35mm f/1.8, is a USB-C Port on the lens mount. This allows you to use a smartphone app or a desktop app to quickly and easily update firmware. This is so much easier than having to download a file to your memory card and installing lens updates via the camera, which is how most native lenses have to be updated. The manual aperture ring features click and clickless operation via a switch on the side, so you can easily see what aperture you’re using at a glance. The focusing ring is smooth and offers comfortable resistance, making manual focus a breeze. It’s also wide enough to rotate using gloves, although, being a compact lens, it’s narrower than what you’d expect on a larger and faster prime lens. Autofocus (AF) is reasona

item.title: NASA’s CHAPEA Crew “Returns” to Earth
item.description: NASA/James Blair The four-member Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) crew poses outside for the first time in more than a year following the end of their simulated Mars journey on Oct. 31, 2026. Crew members Matthew Montgomery (left), James Spicer (middle left), Ross Elder (middle right), and Ellen Ellis (right) spent more than a year testing systems, maintaining crops, managing limited resources and communication delays, conducting extravehicular activities and more in efforts to help NASA better understand how crews adapt to long-duration stays. Insights from their experiences will help NASA design its future Moon Base and plan for missions on Mars. Image credit: NASA/James Blair

item.title: Stumbling block: Wirtz's and Liverpool’s costly struggles against tight defences | Andrew Beasley
item.description: Credit to Arsenal for restricting opportunities at Anfield but Iraola will need his side to learn to unpick low backlines Liverpool did not have a shot on target in their 1-0 defeat by Arsenal on Sunday, according to Opta, the first time they have drawn this type of blank in a Premier League game at Anfield since records began in 2003-04. They did not find the target in a goalless draw at the Emirates Stadium this year either, though in both games they struck the woodwork. The margins tend to be fine when recording statistical outliers. If Alexis Mac Allister’s floated ball from distance into David Raya’s waiting arms had actually counted as a shot, would Andoni Iraola’s side have delivered a markedly better attacking performance? Far more concerning for the Spaniard will be that his team had 52 touches in the Arsenal penalty area (which is good) to create only one Opta‑defined big chance (which is bad). The Premier League average this season is five times more efficient; 10.3 box touches per big chance. Continue reading...

item.title: Coming in 2027: Apple’s $1,000 home robot for FaceTime and switching on lights
item.description: Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room. People who worked on Apple’s robotic projects told The Information that the AI-driven home robot, code-named J595, could be named HomeView Ultra in line with Apple’s new HomeView stationary smart display . The company is reportedly aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027, although development delays may push that back to 2028. The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project. The Information describes Apple’s engineers as trying to give the robot more capabilities beyond being a “fancy way to make FaceTime calls” in order to justify a high price tag, even as the team has spent years refining the software and incorporating more AI technologies. Read full article Comments

item.title: What’s Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips from NASA
item.description: Skywatching Skywatching Home What’s Up Meteor Showers Eclipses Daily Moon Guide More Tips & Guides Skywatching FAQ Night Sky Network Meteor Showers, a Spacecraft Milestone, and a Supermoon Catch Taurid and Leonid meteors, spot Mars near Jupiter, celebrate Voyager 1’s light-day milestone, and watch November’s supermoon. Skywatching Highlights Around Nov. 5: Southern Taurids peak; occasional bright fireballs Around Nov. 12: Northern Taurids peak; around five meteors per hour under ideal conditions Nov. 15-16: Mars and Jupiter appear 1.2 degrees apart before sunrise Nov. 17: Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day activation Nov. 17-18: Leonids before dawn after moonset; up to around 15 meteors per hour under ideal conditions Nov. 24: Full supermoon; first in a series of three consecutive supermoons A full Moon rises over Vasquez Rocks Natural Area and Nature Center north of Los Angeles, California, on June 24, 2021. Credit: NASA/Preston Dyches Transcript A month of meteor showers … a close pairing of Mars and Jupiter … and a supermoon! That’s What’s Up for November. November offers a buffet of opportunities to see a meteor streak across the sky! The Southern Taurids peak around November 5th, followed by the Northern Taurids around November 12th. Those names refer to the two areas in the constellation Taurus, where the meteors appear to originate. Each Taurid shower produces only a handful of meteors per hour—around five, under ideal conditions—but an occasional bright fireball can make the wait worthwhile. A sky chart showing where to look for the Leonids in November 2026. NASA/JPL-Caltech Next up are the Leonids. For the best viewing times, try the early morning hours of November 17th and 18th, after the Moon sets. Under ideal conditions, the shower could produce around 15 meteors per hour, though most viewers will see fewer. To level up your viewing experience, you will want to find a dark location, give your eyes about half an hour to adjust, and take in as much sky as you can. Around mid-month, there’s another reason to head outside early. On the mornings of November 15th and 16th, look southeast before sunrise to see Mars and Jupiter close together. A sky chart showing Mars and Jupiter close in the night sky. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech They’ll appear about 1.2 degrees apart—a little more than the width of two full Moons side by side. Jupiter is the brighter point of light, with reddish Mars nearby. Both planets are easy to see with the unaided eye. They’re still far apart in space, but from Earth, they appear almost side by side. Watch over several mornings to see them draw closer together – and then go their separate ways. Artist’s rendering of a NASA Voyager spacecraft traveling through interstellar space. item.content:encoded: Skywatching Skywatching Home What’s Up Meteor Showers Eclipses Daily Moon Guide More Tips & Guides Skywatching FAQ Night Sky Network Meteor Showers, a Spacecraft Milestone, and a Supermoon Catch Taurid and Leonid meteors, spot Mars near Jupiter, celebrate Voyager 1’s light-day milestone, and watch November’s supermoon. Skywatching Highlights Around Nov. 5: Southern Taurids peak; occasional bright fireballs Around Nov. 12: Northern Taurids peak; around five meteors per hour under ideal conditions Nov. 15-16: Mars and Jupiter appear 1.2 degrees apart before sunrise Nov. 17: Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day activation Nov. 17-18: Leonids before dawn after moonset; up to around 15 meteors per hour under ideal conditions Nov. 24: Full supermoon; first in a series of three consecutive supermoons A full Moon rises over Vasquez Rocks Natural Area and Nature Center north of Los Angeles, California, on June 24, 2021. Credit: NASA/Preston Dyches Transcript A month of meteor showers … a close pairing of Mars and Jupiter … and a supermoon! That’s What’s Up for November. November offers a buffet of opportunities to see a meteor streak across the sky! The Southern Taurids peak around November 5th, followed by the Northern Taurids around November 12th. Those names refer to the two areas in the constellation Taurus, where the meteors appear to originate. Each Taurid shower produces only a handful of meteors per hour—around five, under ideal conditions—but an occasional bright fireball can make the wait worthwhile. A sky chart showing where to look for the Leonids in November 2026. NASA/JPL-Caltech Next up are the Leonids. For the best viewing times, try the early morning hours of November 17th and 18th, after the Moon sets. Under ideal conditions, the shower could produce around 15 meteors per hour, though most viewers will see fewer. To level up your viewing experience, you will want to find a dark location, give your eyes about half an hour to adjust, and take in as much sky as you can. Around mid-month, there’s another reason to head outside early. On the mornings of November 15th and 16th, look southeast before sunrise to see Mars and Jupiter close together. A sky chart showing Mars and Jupiter close in the night sky. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech They’ll appear about 1.2 degrees apart—a little more than the width of two full Moons side by side. Jupiter is the brighter point of light, with reddish Mars nearby. Both planets are easy to see with the unaided eye. They’re still far apart in space, but from Earth, they appear almost side by side. Watch over several mornings to see them draw closer together – and then go their separate ways. Artist’s rendering of a NASA Voyager spacecraft traveling through interstellar space. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech This month, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft will reach a historic milestone, becoming the first human-made object to travel one light-day from Earth. That means a signal traveling at the speed of light takes 24 hours to reach the spacecraft – and another 24 hours for us to hear back from it! If you want to imagine where Voyager 1 is currently traveling, look in the direction of the constellation Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer. A night sky chart highlights the location of Voyager 1 within the constellation Ophiuchus on November 17 around 5 p.m., looking toward the western horizon. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech And on November 17th, join us in celebrating this milestone by participating in our Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day activation. Learn more at nasa.gov/voyager . On November 24th, the evening sky will be lit by a supermoon. Because the Moon’s orbit is slightly oval, its distance from Earth changes. When it’s closer, the full Moon appears larger and brighter than average – though the difference can be subtle. This kicks off a series of three consecutive supermoons in November, December, and January. Look east around sunset to watch it rise. It may look even bigger near the horizon, but that’s the Moon illusion —a common effect with any full Moon. Here are the phases of the Moon for November: Moon phases for November 2026, showing the dates for Third Quarter, New Moon, First Quarter, Full “Supermoon,” and a concluding Third Quarter in Pacific Time. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech You can stay up to date on all of NASA’s missions exploring the solar system and beyond at NASA Science . I’m Raquel Villanueva from NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory and that’s What’s Up this month. Learn More and Get Involved Night Sky Network The Night Sky Network is a nationwide coalition of amateur astronomy clubs bringing the science, technology, and inspiration of NASA’s missions to the general public. item.title: French student protests: 'Illiberal' Macron govt dismisses social movement as 'urban violence'
item.description: Jennie Shin is pleased to welcome Éric Fassin, Sociologist and Professor at Université Paris 8. “In a democracy, elections are very important, but it’s not the end of democracy. It’s the beginning,” explains Fassin. He interprets France’s student protest movement growing into a challenge to socioeconomic policy and what he describes as an “illiberal turn” in government. Connecting the treatment of working-class, racialized youth with wider restrictions on dissent, he argues that racism and democratic participation are central to understanding the unrest. His analysis also challenges the attribution of responsibility to the left, placing the government’s response within a broader debate over the normalization of oppressive measures and the far right.

item.title: Claude’s new rules against game cloning won’t stop the AI copying boom
item.description: Last week, Anthropic introduced a new system prompt designed to stop its Claude models from re-creating specific, existing video games. While that move could help shield Anthropic from some liability, it's unlikely to slow much of the massive wave of AI-assisted game porting and copying that has emerged in recent months. A social media user and AI decompilation enthusiast going by the name "chasm" was among the first to note the prompt change late last week, saying a new rule seemed to be added to the Claude Code prompt on or around October 27. That rule—included in a json file under the name "tengu_heron_brook"—reads as follows: Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original. XDA later independently verified that the new rule appears in version 2.1.314 of the Claude Code binary, which was released on October 30 . XDA also reported that the "tengu_heron_brook" rule had been used for other purposes in earlier versions and that the Claude Opus 5.5 model specifically seemed to have its own distinct and independent instructions restricting game recreations as part of its system prompt bundle. Read full article Comments

item.title: Marvell wants to be a copper topper, bets $115B on photonics leader to push optical networking
item.description: Hoping to dominate the next phase of AI networking, Marvell Technology plans to acquire photonics giant Lumentum in an all-stock deal valued at $115 billion. The move will fill several key gaps in Marvell's photonics portfolio, particularly with regard to high-performance laser sources, optical transceivers, optical circuit switches, and specialized compound semiconductor manufacturing capabilities involving indium phosphide. Higher speed interconnects combined with larger compute domains are the driving forces behind the move to photonics. As interconnects push beyond 400 Gbps per lane, copper interconnects are being pushed to their limit, necessitating denser, hotter rack systems. Optics offer a reprieve from these scaling laws. Traditional copper wire can only maintain a 400 Gbps signal over about 1.25 meters. Every time the per lane speed doubles, the reach is halved. Photonics are largely immune to this and can push that signal over kilometers, enabling infrastructure providers to scale their systems across entire aisles, while also reducing the power and cooling requirements of each individual rack. Due to close in the first half of 2028, the all-stock transaction comes as AI infrastructure builders, including Nvidia and AMD, eye larger rack-scale systems, which will rely heavily on optical interconnects to stitch hundreds and even thousands of GPUs together into a single compute domain for training or inference. At Computex 2026 in Taipei earlier this year, Jensen Huang predicted that Marvell's long-term investments in photonics would catapult the IP house to a $1 trillion valuation. That hasn't happened just yet – the company’s market cap currently sits at just $180 billion – but it seems Marvell isn't above buying its way to the finish line by snapping up optics vendors before the AI boom sends their valuations skyrocketing. As we've previously reported , the move to optical scale up networks has fueled a flurry of investment in optics, silicon photonics development, and manufacturing. Nvidia itself invested $2 billion into Lumentum just eight months ago to bolster its optics manufacturing capacity. The limiting factor up to this point has been power. When Nvidia unveiled its first Blackwell-based rack systems in 2024, Huang noted the company specifically avoided optics as they would have added 20 kW of additional power draw to a system that already consumed 120 kW under load. In the years since then, Marvell has invested heavily in next-gen optics tech. One of the most notable acquisitions came in February 2026, when the company paid about $3.5 billion for photonic interconnect developer Celestial AI. Celestial's tech opened the door to more efficient optics integrations including near- and co-packaged optical interconnects that used a fraction of the power of conventional pluggable optics used in scale out networks. Marvell's Lumentum buy will position the IP house as a one-stop shop for AI infrastructure providers' photonics needs. ®

item.title: OpenAI pitches data center power plants as a way to protect nearby areas
item.description: In an announcement on Monday , OpenAI says it will pilot its "Grid Protectors Program" at an upcoming data center in Effingham County, Georgia, where the company promises to free up to 1,000 megawatts of power during extreme weather or emergencies, enough to power air conditioners in around 700,000 homes. The announcement comes as opposition to data centers spreads across the US, in response to massive projects that have begun development and construction, frequently with little or no input from local residents. In Utah, residents protested after Box Elder County commissioners signed off on a data center expected to consume more than double … Read the full story at The Verge.
