item.title: Voyager 1 gives controllers the silent treatment
item.description: Voyager 1 gave controllers the silent treatment for a few days this month before resuming communication weeks before the spacecraft reaches the one-light-day milestone. The incident happened on October 18: NASA's Deep Space Network (DSN) couldn't detect a signal from the probe. On October 19, on the next scheduled communication attempt, there was still nothing. Was this it? Had the decades-long galactic venture finally ended? Things are operating on a knife's edge for the two veteran spacecraft, which will reach their half-century next year. Voyager 2 suffered an antenna pointing issue in 2023, and a low power condition caused Voyager 1 to unexpectedly turn off one of its two radio transmitters. The good news is that on October 20, the signal reappeared, leaving engineers wondering why Voyager 1 temporarily went silent. Thus far, it seems a group of thrusters went offline and their backups were turned on. This could indicate onboard computers detected a problem and put the spacecraft into a safe mode. Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, said: "This is the first time we've seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected. "We're relieved to be back in contact with Voyager 1 and are eager to understand what happened." The Register spoke to Badaruddin in 2024 , where he described the challenges of working with the veteran spacecraft, but he reckoned the work was the "best job at JPL." The twin Voyager spacecraft have recently been through a procedure dubbed the "Big Bang," where controllers turned off onboard devices and switched to lower power alternatives. The result will extend the lifetime of the spacecraft by a few more years and postpone further instrument deactivation. It was completed first on Voyager 2, and then Voyager 1, six weeks later in September. However, the brief lapse in communication highlights that despite the ingenuity of the team that keep the spacecraft running, the project must eventually come to an end. In 2026, Suzanne Dodd, Project Manager for the Voyager project, told The Register what the end would look like . She said, "We're just going to one day not hear the signal from the DSN, and we're going to rush around and make sure that it's not something on the ground." Months of listening will follow, before engineers throw in the towel and declare the mission over. And then? Maybe a farewell message sent to the last known location. Thankfully, in this case, the signal returned, so no need for a goodbye transmission just yet. In a few weeks, Voyager 1 will be so far away that it will take a full 24 hours for commands to reach it and another 24 hours for a response to reach Earth. Communications blip notwithstanding, there is every chance both Voyager spacecraft will still be operational as they pass their half-century milestone next year and, technology and funding permitting, continue sending data to Earth

item.title: What happened this month at the European Space Agency? (October 2026)
item.description: Video: 00:04:30 October was a month of discoveries and milestones. ESA’s Rosalind Franklin rover team trained in Spain’s desert, preparing for Mars. Our Smile mission captured the full ring of northern lights around Earth, while Mars Express uncovered new clues about a giant Martian cloud. ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot returned to Earth after 237 days in space, and Hera captured its first images of the asteroids it will study to help protect our planet. Meanwhile, ESA welcomed thousands of visitors for Open Days and teamed up with Pokémon to bring space science to new audiences. Here’s a look at what space had in store for Europe this October.

item.title: 'Star Trek's' William Shatner and George Takei honor the death of Walter Koenig
item.description: null This has been a pretty rough week for " Star Trek " royalty on this 60th anniversary year with the deaths of both Walter Koenig , "Star Trek's" Lt. Pavel Chekov on Sunday, Oct. 25 and Patrick Stewart , the storied sci-fi property's Captain Jean Luc-Picard on Wednesday, Oct. 28. With the passing of Walter Koenig at the age of 90 this past week, franchise luminaries of all degrees are coming out with heartfelt condolences, kind words of remembrance, and tearful reflections. William Shatner, 95, and George Takei, 89, represent the final remaining members of the U.S.S. Enterprise's core crew from "Star Trek: The Original Series" and they both took to social media to express their deep sorrow over losing one of their fellow travelers in the final frontier. Walter Koenig played as Pavel Chekov in six "Star Trek" feature films plus a small role in "Star Trek: Generations." (Image credit: Paramount) "I am deeply saddened to learn of Walter Koenig’s passing," Shatner posted on Instagram . "Although we did not know each other well away from the set, we shared the later seasons of the original 'Star Trek' series and the six films that followed. What I observed, and what so many fans have expressed over the years, was a man who genuinely loved the 'Star Trek' community. "At conventions, Walter was rarely content to remain behind a signing table. He preferred to be among the people who had kept 'Star Trek' alive for so many decades. That kind of genuine connection is rare, and it will be remembered by everyone who came into contact with him. "My condolences to his family, his friends, and the countless fans whose lives he touched." Walter Koenig co-starred in "Star Trek: The Original Series" for two seasons (Image credit: Paramount) George Takei, who portrayed Lt. Hikaru Sulu and co-starred with Koenig on two seasons of "The Original Series" from 1967-69, as well as six subsequent "Star Trek" feature films, offered similar thoughts in memoriam. "My heart is heavy. Walter Koenig, our Ensign Pavel Chekov, passed away early today," Takei shared on his Instagram page. "Walter and I met on the bridge of the Enterprise in the 1960s, and we stayed friends for nearly six decades. When Brad and I married in 2008, Walter stood beside us as our best man. Just last month, on Sept. 14, he turned 90, on the same day Brad and I celebrated our 18th wedding anniversary. I will always treasure that he and I shared that date. "Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend. To the fans who loved him for so many years, thank you. He loved you too. "Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course."

item.title: A New Map of ‘Empty’ Space Challenges a Tranquil Picture of the Galaxy
item.description: You might imagine space to be empty. But the seeming void contains a barely perceptible fog of hydrogen and other neutral atoms. In 2020, NASA’s New Horizons spacecraft, having passed the orbit of Pluto, measured a proxy for the amount of hydrogen around it. In the area between stars in our galaxy — the “interstellar medium,” or ISM — New Horizons found around 130 hydrogen atoms per liter of space. Source

item.title: On this day in space! Oct. 30, 1964: NASA's weird Lunar Landing Research Vehicle takes 1st test flight to help Apollo astronauts land on the moon
item.description: null On October 30, 1964, NASA's Lunar Landing Research Vehicle, or LLRV, took to the skies for the first time. The LLRV was a bizarre, four-legged flying contraption commonly known as the "Flying Bedstead." NASA used it to simulate moon landings and liftoffs on Earth to prepare for Apollo 11 , the first crewed lunar landing. The first person to give it a whirl was the X-15 pilot Joe Walker . During this test flight, he reached an altitude of about 10 feet, and he hovered there for about a minute. He did this two more times that same day. In all, he completed more than 30 test flights with the LLRV. These test flights took place at NASA's Dryden Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. That facility has since been renamed the Armstrong Flight Research Center after Neil Armstrong , who also piloted — and famously crashed — the "Flying Bedstead" before he went to the moon. The first Lunar Landing Research Vehicle is pictured during a test flight at NASA's Dryden Flight Research Center in California. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered Over 60 years ago this LLRV test flight was a critical step toward landing humans on the moon for the first time, a historic moment that both served an important political purpose while also showcasing the result of monumental scientific and technical progress. While images from this test flight might look like the team are having a bit of fun out in the desert, and perhaps they were, it was also deadly serious. The astronauts who signed onto these crewed missions were doing something that had never been attempted. They were putting their lives on the line for this progress, and this testing was a major piece in reassuring them and NASA that lunar landing could be accomplished, and safely. Today, as we return humans to the moon with NASA's Artemis program, we see parallels between testing done over 60 years ago and testing today. Right now, SpaceX and Blue Origin are testing their lunar landers for crewed lunar landings in the near-future. While we have now been to the moon and have safely and successfully landed humans before, these tests remain critical for the safety and success of the missions. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.content:encoded: null On October 30, 1964, NASA's Lunar Landing Research Vehicle, or LLRV, took to the skies for the first time. The LLRV was a bizarre, four-legged flying contraption commonly known as the "Flying Bedstead." NASA used it to simulate moon landings and liftoffs on Earth to prepare for Apollo 11 , the first crewed lunar landing. The first person to give it a whirl was the X-15 pilot Joe Walker . During this test flight, he reached an altitude of about 10 feet, and he hovered there for about a minute. He did this two more times that same day. In all, he completed more than 30 test flights with the LLRV. These test flights took place at NASA's Dryden Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. That facility has since been renamed the Armstrong Flight Research Center after Neil Armstrong , who also piloted — and famously crashed — the "Flying Bedstead" before he went to the moon. The first Lunar Landing Research Vehicle is pictured during a test flight at NASA's Dryden Flight Research Center in California. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered Over 60 years ago this LLRV test flight was a critical step toward landing humans on the moon for the first time, a historic moment that both served an important political purpose while also showcasing the result of monumental scientific and technical progress. item.title: AlpineBSD announced – an AI-free FOSS OS
item.description: Just days after Daemonarchy, there's another new OS in the BSD family – and one that is heading determinedly in almost the opposite direction. AlpineBSD is so new that it barely exists yet. There are no installation media available, though it's possible to manually bootstrap an installation . What AlpineBSD does already have is an AI policy, and the plan is to avoid "the output of generative AI models (e.g. LLMs)" as far as possible: "Any software whose code, documentation, binaries, or other assets include, in any part, the output of a generative AI tool such as an LLM, is considered 'tainted' for our purposes." The core idea is to combine the kernel of NetBSD with "a userspace inspired by Alpine Linux and the objective of making it possible to use as little AI-generated software as possible." Back in 2024 , the NetBSD project made its position on AI plain. Its commit guidelines say that "code generated by a Large Language Model […] is presumed to be tainted code." Back in July, Linus Torvalds stated that "Linux is not one of those anti-AI projects ". Since then, NetBSD has seen a spike in donations and interest . For someone mainly used to Linux, trying to install NetBSD is a little like hopping in a time machine to 30 years ago, and we speak from personal experience of Linux in the mid-1990s. As we mentioned when Slackware turned 30 a few years ago, back in 1996, this vulture tried Slackware 3.0 on his own hardware, and we never did manage to install it. We tried NetBSD 11 a couple of months ago , and despite considerable help from the folks on the NetBSD-users mailing list, we failed to get the CDE desktop to start. As an example, installing software on NetBSD is not the easy, comfortable task it is on Linux. It does have a package manager for handling binary packages: it's called pkgin , but as the NetBSD FAQ mentions , it's an optional extra. You must manually tick a box in the setup program to install pkgin with the rest of the OS, and when we tried NetBSD 9.3 four years ago , we didn't know that, overlooked that checkbox, and had to find a way to add pkgin later. (It is quite tricky to install a package manager when you don't have a package manager to install it with.) This time around, we discovered that pkgin sometimes doesn't complete the installation process for you – it just leaves a text file in a destination directory somewhere, and you're expected to know that, go there, read it, and do any further steps yourself. The NetBSD community has been quietly going its own way since 1993. It has its own ideas about what is normal, and its users expect that. Some folks on the mailing list told us that they never use binary packages anyway – they compile what they need from source code. AlpineBSD's ports repository and source code are hosted on Sourcehut, under the account of sircmpwn , better known as Drew DeVault . We have quoted DeVault a few times over the years: we've often found that his views align with our own in various ways… such

Some folks on the mailing list told us that they never use binary packages anyway – they compile what they need from source code. AlpineBSD's ports repository and source code are hosted on Sourcehut, under the account of sircmpwn , better known as Drew DeVault . We have quoted DeVault a few times over the years: we've often found that his views align with our own in various ways… such as about t he best laptops ever made , and on simplicity in Linux distro design , or even on dot-com billionaires at FOSDEM . Alpine's tools are quite well-suited to being adapted to other systems. We have previously mentioned the use of its packaging tool, APK, in the GNU-free Chimera Linux , which uses much of the FreeBSD userland, and also in Adélie Linux . We will follow AlpineBSD with interest. There's strong appeal in the plan of combining perhaps the best-known, longest-established AI-free Unix-like kernel with the user-facing parts of pretty much the smallest and cleanest Linux distro there is. The AI advocates often warn LLM skeptics that they risk being left behind. Well, here's an OS for those who don't want to surf the AI wave. ®

item.title: Ghostly Cat's Head Nebula haunts the cosmos | Space photo of the day for Oct. 30, 2026
item.description: null Three views of the Cat's Head Nebula. A visible light image captured by NASA's Hubble Space Telescope (left); a mid-infrared image taken by James Webb Space Telescope (center); and the James Webb Space Telescope's near-infrared view (right). (Image credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI; Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI)) This "cat's head" would work perfectly in a witch's cauldron, glowing red "eyes" and all. Just in time for Halloween, we have new, ghostly views of the Cat's Eye Nebula haunting the outer reaches of the cosmos. What is it? This nebula earned its name from its distinctive "cat's head" shape, which you can see on the left-hand side of these two images snapped by both the Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes . In these new images, you can even see the cat's glowing red "eye," which experts suggest could be a young star trapped in the nebula's dusty clutches. A visible light image of the Cat's Head Nebula captured by NASA's Hubble Space Telescope. The nebula's distinctive "cat's head" shape was formed over eons by intense ultraviolet radiation and winds of gases streaming from massive stars in the Carina Nebula. (Image credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI; Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI)) Found about 7,500 light-years away from Earth, this star-forming region can be found within the larger Carina Nebula . As the stars in the Carina Nebula continue to form, grow and evolve over time, the Nebula itself will change and eventually, this "cat's head" won't look much like a cat anymore. But for now, we can enjoy this vision of a domestic cat somehow depicted in this colossal tour of gas and dust. Why is it incredible? As a special Halloween treat, we have not one, but three new images of the cosmic cat's head. In the snapshot captured by Hubble, we can see the nebula in visible light. This view shows the nebula as a brown pillar of dust embedded in a hazy, almost rainbow field of dust and gas. These colors are captured through Hubble's filters that can see the light coming from oxygen, hydrogen and sulfur and the light scattered by nebula dust. JWST also took a look at this cat's head, observing the nebula in near- and mid-infrared wavelengths. By looking at the same objects in space through different wavelengths and with different instruments and telescopes, we can uncover completely new and different details about these far-off celestial objects.

item.title: NASA ponders a Hubble servicing mission or a controlled deorbit
item.description: NASA has posted a contract opportunity notice, also known as a request for information, from commercial space orgs who can service the Hubble Space Telescope. Hubble was always looked after by NASA astronauts flying on the Space Shuttle, yet the last Hubble Space Telescope (HST) servicing mission was the STS-125 Space Shuttle flight, launched on May 11, 2009. At the time, scientists hoped the mission would add another five years of operational life to the venerable spacecraft. Almost 17 years on, the HST (aka Hubble) is still delivering science. However, time is running out for the observatory. NASA reckons there is a 10 percent chance it could reenter the Earth's atmosphere by September 2032, rising to 50 percent by December 2033. As the end of the Swift mission showed, increased solar activity can cause greater-than-anticipated atmospheric drag. Also, like Swift, Hubble has no propulsion system, and so when it reenters (as it will, without intervention), the reentry will be uncontrolled. Hubble is sufficiently massive that there is a remote chance somebody on the ground could have a very bad day when that happens. As such, one mission option suggested by NASA is a vehicle to grapple the observatory and perform a controlled reentry and disposal. However, there are other options. Something to boost the telescope's orbit up to at least 600 km, or another to "enhance its ongoing performance and increase its resilience and expected on-orbit lifetime." Both are intriguing options, and important since, as NASA acknowledges, no replacement for Hubble is expected before the 2040s, when the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) could become operational. Despite the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Nancy Roman Space Telescope, Hubble remains in high demand, with NASA reporting a 7:1 oversubscription. Before becoming NASA Administrator, Jared Isaacman advocated a SpaceX mission to boost the Hubble, but the idea was ultimately rejected. Similar plans could now be dusted off. NASA's requirement is for a mission to occur by 2032, and not harm the Hubble. A soft-capture mechanism was fitted to Hubble during the STS-125 mission, which will mean docking with the spacecraft will be easier than the grappling planned for Swift. Then, the question is what to do with it. A controlled reentry is one option. The other options – boosting to a higher altitude or "enhance its ongoing performance and increase its resilience" are intriguing. Northrop Grumman's Mission Extension Vehicle (MEV) , for example, is capable of on-orbit servicing and extending the lifetime of satellites. The Hubble is an order of magnitude more challenging, but the technological hurdles can be overcome with time and funding. Last year, The Register spoke with Dr John Grunsfeld, one of the astronauts (now retired) who worked on Hubble during the STS-125 mission. Grunsfeld told us that the veteran spacecraft faced death by a thousand cuts as its budget was whittled away. The observatory itself

Before becoming NASA Administrator, Jared Isaacman advocated a SpaceX mission to boost the Hubble, but the idea was ultimately rejected. Similar plans could now be dusted off. NASA's requirement is for a mission to occur by 2032, and not harm the Hubble. A soft-capture mechanism was fitted to Hubble during the STS-125 mission, which will mean docking with the spacecraft will be easier than the grappling planned for Swift. Then, the question is what to do with it. A controlled reentry is one option. The other options – boosting to a higher altitude or "enhance its ongoing performance and increase its resilience" are intriguing. Northrop Grumman's Mission Extension Vehicle (MEV) , for example, is capable of on-orbit servicing and extending the lifetime of satellites. The Hubble is an order of magnitude more challenging, but the technological hurdles can be overcome with time and funding. Last year, The Register spoke with Dr John Grunsfeld, one of the astronauts (now retired) who worked on Hubble during the STS-125 mission. Grunsfeld told us that the veteran spacecraft faced death by a thousand cuts as its budget was whittled away. The observatory itself recently switched from three to one gyro mode (the telescope uses gyros to control where it is pointed) to eke out a few more years of operational life. At this point, NASA is looking for information and comment – this isn't a request for proposals. There is no indication of how much the agency expects to pay. However, the timescale is immutable. Without intervention, Hubble will make an uncontrolled reentry in the coming years. ®

item.title: Here Are 5 Reasons to Make Heineken Lagos Fashion Week 2026 a Must-Experience
item.description: You come for the collections, take notes on the street style, and leave with a camera roll full of inspiration. That is part of the thrill of Heineken Lagos Fashion Week, there is always something exciting that makes you stop and think, “I would never have thought of that.” Rooted in cities and the cultures that shape them, Heineken finds inspiration in the people, creativity and experiences that give each city its character. This year, through City of Cities: Where Taste Rules, the brand celebrates Lagos’ distinctive energy with experiences spanning the Heineken Runway showcase, Heineken Lounge, the Nigerian debut of Heineken Studio and the Heineken After Party. Curious? Here are five reasons to make room for Heineken in your Fashion Week plans: A Celebration of Fashion and Creative Expression Ever wondered what happens when different styles, ideas and creative perspectives come together? Here is your chance to find out. Last year, the City of Cities showcase featured a 46-piece collection curated by Omoyemi Akerele , bringing together designers including Atafo, Nkwo, Orange Culture , Dimeji Ilori and Eki Kere . From raffia and sequins to intricate hand-beaded details, the collection reflected the breadth of talent and craftsmanship within African fashion. In 2026, Heineken continues to celebrate the creative expressions that shape Lagos’ identity, building on its connection to cities and the cultures that make them unique through City of Cities: Where Taste Rules. Discover a New Expression of Taste at Heineken Studio Fashion Week is a place for discovering what is next, and this year, Heineken is bringing that spirit of exploration to taste and socializing. Last year, the Heineken District served as the week’s fashion-focused experience zone, hosting live recordings of fan-favourite podcasts from Tea with Tay to Off Air with Gbemi & Toolz and Toke Moments . Guest speakers and the hosts unpacked everything from sustainability to the evolution of style in Nigeria. Alongside it, the Drip’o’meter put a curated spotlight on the week’s most fashion-forward attendees. This year, Heineken is taking that spirit of exploration even further. Making its Nigerian debut, Heineken Studio will offer guests a closer look at the brand’s playground of innovation, exploring new ways to brew, serve and experience lager. It is one of the ways Heineken is bringing its innovation to life, inviting guests to discover what happens when brewing expertise meets a willingness to try something different. Last year, Lagos Fashion Week welcomed designers, creatives, culture enthusiasts and international star Ciara, bringing further global attention to the city’s fashion scene. This year, Heineken’s presence across the event creates more opportunities

item.title: AI projects not paying off? Keep at it, says Uni Productivity Institute
item.description: The University of Manchester is scrutinizing why growing adoption of AI tools has so far failed to translate into the forecast productivity gains, however, researchers are struggling to give easy answers to close the "AI ambition gap." In a report, also called “ The AI Ambition Gap ,” the UK university’s Productivity Institute mulls over the advances that have been made in AI and the expanding adoption of it, and sets out what business leaders and policymakers can do to realize the potential benefits. The report was commissioned by IT services biz Bytes Technology Group . One reason for the lack of results is that organizations have invested heavily up front on retraining staff, reorganizing the way they work and other adjustments. Those costs show up straight away, yet the payback doesn’t come until later. Another reason, the report suggests, is that AI tools can raise productivity at the level of individual tasks, but these gains do not automatically translate into greater productivity across a worker’s whole role or the entire organization. It cites the example of software developers using GitHub Copilot who completed around 26 percent more tasks, and professionals using ChatGPT for routine writing and analysis that reduced task completion time by 40 percent while improving the quality of the output by 18 percent. However, a study of AI dev tools found these have increased coding activity by approximately 240 percent, while the number of actual software releases has only grown by about 30 percent. The gap is due to humans still needing to check and test their work before release. High task exposure to AI does not automatically make a worker more productive, the researchers say. Jobs typically combine automatable activities with tasks that require judgement, coordination, client interaction and critical thinking. As AI removes or accelerates some activities, those complementary human tasks become the constraint on time saving and the translation of task-level gains into greater productivity Job outcomes therefore depend on task composition and complementary human expertise, the report continues. It suggests AI may in part displace labor from existing tasks, while also creating new tasks in which workers retain a comparative advantage. This could be good news for the UK, the researchers state. Compared with five other nations (US, Brazil, Colombia, India and South Africa), Blighty has the highest share of workers in occupations with both high exposure to AI and "high complementarity," it claims. This is in part related to the country’s large financial and professional business service sectors, which are characterized by a high share of cognitive occupations. This is just as well, as the government is pinning its hopes on using AI to drive economic recovery in a strategy outlined at the start of last year. It suggests AI may in part displace labor from existing tasks, while also creating new tasks in which workers retain a comparative advantage. This could be good news for the UK, the researchers state. Compared with five other nations (US, Brazil, Colombia, India and South Africa), Blighty has the highest share of workers in occupations with both high exposure to AI and "high complementarity," it claims. This is in part related to the country’s large financial and professional business service sectors, which are characterized by a high share of cognitive occupations. This is just as well, as the government is pinning its hopes on using AI to drive economic recovery in a strategy outlined at the start of last year. Britain's AI sector is relatively large by European standards, and the report cites recent OECD estimates that high-exposure economies such as the UK and the US could see annual labor productivity gains of between 0.4 and 1.3 percentage points. Even an annual uplift of around 0.5 to 0.7 percentage points would represent a significant step change relative to the UK’s stalled productivity performance over the past decade, it says, if this effect is sustained. The Productivity Institute lists several "mutually reinforcing enablers" to help organizations close the ambition gap it identifies. None is particularly surprising, especially if you have read other reports advising on corporate success with AI adoption. One is management setting strategic direction for the organization, another is strengthening worker capabilities through greater knowledge and data literacy to help organizations turn individual insight into shared learning. Others include implementing AI governance and focusing on applications that can create new products, improve core processes or solve previously intractable problems. "AI's productivity potential becomes real when faster tasks lead to better performance across the business," said Bart van Ark, professor at The Productivity Institute and lead author on the report. "The ambition gap lies between those individual efficiencies and sustained business results. Closing it requires firms to invest in management, skills and the redesign of workflows alongside the technology." The conclusion is that companies must have faith and keep investing in AI, and eventually the benefits will come if you are doing the right things. These include focusing on high-value use cases linked to strategy, customer value and operational bottlenecks, plus treating AI as a workplace redesign. Policymakers could help out businesses here by assisting identifying relevant opportunities, the report says, to reduce adoption risks and uncertainty. Other reports published this week were more defined in their message: Gartner said 75 percent of corporate board members have yet to see any productivity gains or reduce costs from AI use, and private equity biz Apollo Global Management reckons only the biggest tech vendors are enjoying some sort of AI payoff. ®

item.title: NHS quango warns of risk to GP patient data after website vendor collapse
item.description: The UK's top health quango has called on family doctors to figure out how to preserve health information and get in touch with patients after a website provider collapsed earlier this month. NHS England has taken the unusual step of writing to GPs, warning them of the risks to patient information and continuity of service following the disruption to potentially hundreds of practices around the UK. Silicon Practice Digital Health Solutions — owned by Schappit Ltd — has gone into administration . Reports suggest some GP websites have gone offline completely. Practice managers fear the extra workload and are struggling to stand up alternative forms of communication since the switch to digital channels. NHS England is the government unit which runs the health service in England, but it is not directly responsible for GP practices, the vast majority of which are independent contractors. Nonetheless, the quango’s CTO, Kevin Humphries, wrote to practices and NHS organizations this week outlining his priorities in mitigating the impact of tech service collapse. They include finding ways of preserving any historical patient information, particularly where it has not been moved to clinical systems, managing the online consultation backlog to make sure no additional requests are added, and identifying channels for patient access until new online systems are available. Practices should also consider whether they have a legal obligation to tell the Information Commissioner's Office if the "availability, integrity, confidentiality or recoverability of personal data" is affected, according to the communication seen by The Register . NHS management bodies called Integrated Care Boards are responsible for GP IT service arrangements, making sure they include "clinical safety, data security, cyber security and business continuity assurance across the GP IT supply chain," Humphries said. They need to find someone to lead their recovery plan and contact affected practices and trusts. They should also "work with practices and other impacted organizations to support them in revisiting and assessing whether to enact business continuity and disaster recovery plans," Humphries said. Questions over how an urgent NHS-wide response is required for the collapse of a relatively small supplier may come later. Among them will be the due diligence conducted before Schappit Ltd was added to a government framework in July . GP and open-source tech campaigner Marcus Baw has published a free, open source template for an alternative website should practices want to bring systems in-house. He said the template is based on accessible NHS web standards, and has the same look-and-feel of common NHS websites. "Practices can deploy it for free, and take back in-house control of their own website. It's a replacement website template which practices can set up using Claude Code in the web in an afternoon," he said. ®

item.title: Watch Virgin Galactic's new 'Delta-class' space plane take to the skies for the 1st time (video)
item.description: null Virgin Galactic's first "Delta-class" space plane just made its maiden voyage. The next-gen suborbital vehicle, named Apeiron (Greek for "Boundless"), lifted off for the first time ever on Thursday (Oct. 28). Flying beneath the wings of its carrier aircraft, VMS Eve, Apeiron traveled from Virgin's manufacturing site in Mesa, Arizona, to its launch site, Spaceport America in New Mexico. "Seeing the ship fly beneath Eve to Spaceport America was a moment years in the making," Virgin Galactic CEO Michael Colglazier said in a statement on Thursday . "To our team and our astronaut community: your Spaceship has arrived." Virgin Galactic's first Delta-class space plane, named Apeiron, takes to the skies for the first time on Oct. 28, 2026, beneath the wings of its carrier plane, VMS Eve. (Image credit: Virgin Galactic) Apeiron will undergo a series of checks and tests at Spaceport America, leading up to a planned start of commercial service in the spring of 2027. During those customer flights, Eve will carry Apeiron to an altitude of about 45,000 feet (13,700 meters), then drop the space plane. Apeiron will fire up its onboard rocket motor, which will carry the six-passenger, two-pilot vehicle to suborbital space. Passengers will experience a few minutes of weightlessness and get to see the curve of Earth against the blackness of space before coming down for a runway landing back at Spaceport America. Virgin Galactic has done this before, with its VSS Unity space plane. Unity flew seven commercial suborbital missions during its operational life, which ran from June 2023 to June 2024. Apeiron and other Delta-class planes are built for a much heavier workload, according to Virgin Galactic. "Designed to fly twice per week with a vehicle lifetime of more than 500 missions, each Spaceship in the next-generation fleet is built to support the economics of a scaled commercial operation, with increased flight cadence and a cost profile unprecedented in the industry," company representatives wrote in the same statement. And there will indeed be a fleet, if all goes to plan. The second Delta ship is under construction, for example, and is expected to enter service in mid-2027, according to Virgin Galactic. Apeiron and its Delta-class siblings will need to fly a lot to deal with Virgin Galactic's backlog: Nearly 700 ticket-holders are currently waiting to fly, according to the company . And demand remains high; the latest batch of seats, which were priced at $750,000 apiece, sold out. Virgin plans to sell the next tranche of tickets for $850,000 each, LATTE Luxury News reported . Another look at Apeiron. (Image credit: Virgin Galactic) When Apeiron gets up and running, it will be the only game in town for suborbital space tourists. Virgin Galactic once shared the skies with Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin , which flew paying customers to the final frontier on its New Shepard vehicle. New Shepard conducted 14 crewed suborbital flights between July 2021 and January 2026

item.title: Look up! China's mysterious space plane is visible over the US this week
item.description: null China's secretive space plane is making a series of passes over the United States in the coming days and you could spot it with your own eyes! The mysterious spacecraft, Shenlong, is currently orbiting Earth on its fourth mission . Although we don't know what it's up to, China's space agency has said it is testing technologies that "will pave the way for more convenient and affordable round-trip methods for the peaceful use of space in the future." Under favorable conditions, Shenlong is bright enough to spot with the naked eye, according to Spaceweather.com. But you'll need to set your alarm early, as some of the best viewing opportunities are in the predawn sky. When and where to see China's space plane According to satellite-tracking website Heavens-Above , skywatchers across the U.S. have several opportunities to spot Shenlong between Oct. 30 and early November, weather permitting. Here are some of the most promising high-altitude passes for four major U.S. cities. All times are local, with the end of daylight saving time on Nov. 1 taken into account. Times are approximate and may change. Maximum elevation refers to the spacecraft's highest angle above the horizon, with 90° being directly overhead. Best predicted viewing opportunities City Date Local viewing window Maximum elevation New York Nov. 1 5:20-5:28 a.m. EST 78° Chicago Nov. 3 4:37-4:42 a.m. CST 85° Denver Nov. 2 5:05-5:12 a.m. MST 73° Los Angeles Nov. 2 5:42-5:51 a.m. PST 83° If clouds get in the way (or you forget to set your alarm), don't worry! There are several other opportunities over the coming days. Other promising passes City Date Local viewing window Maximum elevation New York Oct. 31 6:13–6:20 a.m. EDT 52° New York Nov. 2 5:28–5:37 a.m. EST 66° Chicago Oct. 31 6:50–6:59 a.m. CDT 74° Chicago Nov. 2 4:29–4:34 a.m. CST 64° Denver Nov. 1 4:57–5:04 a.m. MST 48° Denver Nov. 3 5:13–5:20 a.m. MST 70° Los Angeles Nov. 5 4:29–4:35 a.m. PST 69° Los Angeles Nov. 6 4:38–4:43 a.m. PST 66° How can I see Shenlong from where I live? These predictions are specific to each city, so your exact viewing times will depend on your viewing location. Shenlong pass over New York on Nov. 1 timings. The highlighted circle is the region where the satellite is at least 10° above your horizon. The size of the circle depends on the height of the satellite. (Image credit: Chris Peat/Heavens-Above) To find out when Shenlong will pass over your location, head to Heavens-Above , enter your location (in the top right corner of the page), then on the homepage look for "satellite database" under the satellites subheader. And search for "PRC TEST SPACECRAFT 4". Select "visible only" to see upcoming passes and click on a date to bring up a detailed sky chart showing the spacecraft's predicted path across the sky, including where to look and when. These predictions are specific to each city, so your exact viewing times will depend on your viewing location. Shenlong pass over New York on Nov. 1 timings. The highlighted circle is the region where the satellite is at least 10° above your horizon. The size of the circle depends on the height of the satellite. And search for "PRC TEST SPACECRAFT 4". Select "visible only" to see upcoming passes and click on a date to bring up a detailed sky chart showing the spacecraft's predicted path across the sky, including where to look and when. What will China's space plane look like? To the naked eye, Shenlong will look like a small, steadily moving point of light, similar to a satellite gliding across the sky. Its brightness can vary significantly. Veteran satellite observer Paul Maley spotted Shenlong from Paarl, South Africa, in February 2026, estimating its brightness at between magnitude +2.5 and +3.5 at its brightest, according to Spaceweather.com. Maley reported that the spacecraft was easily visible to the naked eye under dark, moonless skies, but noted that it could also become much fainter, potentially dropping to magnitude +6. Shenlong is a reusable spacecraft that launches aboard a rocket before eventually returning to Earth for a runway landing, much like the U.S. military's X-37B space plane. China has revealed relatively little about its activities, although the spacecraft has been observed interacting with other objects in orbit. Just days ago, the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency released a remarkable new photograph of Shenlong , offering a rare glimpse into this mysterious spacecraft.

item.title: British intelligence agency misplaced 'thousands' of storage devices, years later still can't say how many
item.description: Thousands of GCHQ storage drives containing sensitive data have been lost for years, and the British signals intelligence agency still cannot explain where they are. According to the Investigatory Powers Commissioner’s Office’s (IPCO) annual report , the missing storage drives have been known to officials for years, and may contain data related to the Investigatory Powers Act (IPA) . "I remain concerned that GCHQ has not yet established a sufficiently clear understanding of the scale, location, and recoverability of lost removable media that may contain IPA-related data, notwithstanding that the underlying issues were first drawn to my attention several years ago," wrote investigatory powers commissioner Lord Brian Leveson. "While I recognize the technical and practical challenges involved, the passage of time without a comprehensive account heightens the importance of sustained senior focus and assured remediation. Given the potential sensitivity of the material involved, I will continue to monitor progress closely.” Described as "a very significant number," the report notes that GCHQ has scoped the maximum number of potentially lost drives, but is unaware of the exact scale of the issue. The agency has embarked on "a program of further work" to locate as many of the lost devices as possible, which includes implementing an automated asset-tracking system by the end of the year. After this is up and running, it said it will be able to provide a more precise number of lost drives. A GCHQ spokesperson told The Register : "As IPCO have reported, our management system for removable media was previously not sufficiently robust to effectively track the items that were registered for use. IPCO are right to note the flaws in the data the system produced, and we have taken action against all their recommendations. "We recognize the importance of security of removable media in our systems, and have a range of measures to mitigate the risks posed by these items. The findings in the report have been addressed comprehensively, and all necessary steps to correct this issue have been taken." Peter Sommer, digital forensics expert and visiting professor at de Montfort and Birmingham City universities, told us: "Bearing in mind the sort of highly sensitive data collected and processed by GCHQ IPCO is right to be very concerned, the more so as the issue is already several years old. Vast quantities of data can be stored on the cheapest lowest cost hard disks and cards. At a much more modest level as an expert witness I know how important it is to keep careful track of the data entrusted to me." Losing important devices is not an achievement that's exclusive to GCHQ. Myriad stories like this have emerged from all corners of the public sector over the years, such as the British Minidstry of Defence misplacing USB drives containing secret information in the mid-noughties, civil servants routinely losing their BlackBerry handsets , and UK police losing thousands of de
item.dc:creator: Connor Jones
item.content:encoded: Thousands of GCHQ storage drives containing sensitive data have been lost for years, and the British signals intelligence agency still cannot explain where they are. According to the Investigatory Powers Commissioner’s Office’s (IPCO) annual report , the missing storage drives have been known to officials for years, and may contain data related to the Investigatory Powers Act (IPA) . "I remain concerned that GCHQ has not yet established a sufficiently clear understanding of the scale, location, and recoverability of lost removable media that may contain IPA-related data, notwithstanding that the underlying issues were first drawn to my attention several years ago," wrote investigatory powers commissioner Lord Brian Leveson. "While I recognize the technical and practical challenges involved, the passage of time without a comprehensive account heightens the importance of sustained senior focus and assured remediation. Given the potential sensitivity of the material involved, I will continue to monitor progress closely.” Described as "a very significant number," the report notes that GCHQ has scoped the maximum number of potentially lost drives, but is unaware of the exact scale of the issue. The agency has embarked on "a program of further work" to locate as many of the lost devices as possible, which includes implementing an automated asset-tracking system by the end of the year. After this is up and running, it said it will be able to provide a more precise number of lost drives. A GCHQ spokesperson told The Register : "As IPCO have reported, our management system for removable media was previously not sufficiently robust to effectively track the items that were registered for use. IPCO are right to note the flaws in the data the system produced, and we have taken action against all their recommendations. "We recognize the importance of security of removable media in our systems, and have a range of measures to mitigate the risks posed by these items. The findings in the report have been addressed comprehensively, and all necessary steps to correct this issue have been taken." Peter Sommer, digital forensics expert and visiting professor at de Montfort and Birmingham City universities, told us: "Bearing in mind the sort of highly sensitive data collected and processed by GCHQ IPCO is right to be very concerned, the more so as the issue is already several years old. Vast quantities of data can be stored on the cheapest lowest cost hard disks and cards. At a much more modest level as an expert witness I know how important it is to keep careful track of the data entrusted to me." Losing important devices is not an achievement that's exclusive to GCHQ. Myriad stories like this have emerged from all corners of the public sector over the years, such as the British Minidstry of Defence misplacing USB drives containing secret information in the mid-noughties, civil servants routinely losing their BlackBerry handsets , and UK police losing thousands of devices , too. The missing storage drives comprise just one of the agency's various transgressions highlighted by IPCO in its report. There are also "significant concerns" over the lax safeguards used to restrict the UK's overseas partners when accessing bulk-intercepted data collected by GCHQ. IPCO was satisfied at how GCHQ ensured its own analysts remained compliant with safeguards around accessing confidential material related to journalism, journalistic sources, and privileged legal information. However, there were concerns around how these same safeguards were applied to its international partners, which have access to its so-called bulk data interception "product." The report notes that most partners were properly restricted from accessing such material, although an internal probe found that there were inadequate arrangements in respect to one partner and their access to journalistic material. Both GCHQ and the overseas agency committed to rectifying the situation. GCHQ was also questioned after a software bug in a web app "used by a relatively small section of the public" misidentified individuals thought to be participating in terrorist activities. The agency identified and reported the flaw in the software, which it used for "target discovery work," and although it only affected a small number of individuals, the errors led to five port stops made under the Terrorism Act and caused "serious prejudice" to the victims. A port stop, for the uninitiated, involves law enforcement detaining a suspect at a UK port, airport, train station, or within one mile of the Northern Ireland border, and can be carried out without suspicion. Once detained, individuals have a legal responsibility to provide passwords to their electronic devices, which can be seized for up to seven days, and in some cases have their biometric markers taken. Failure to comply can lead to a three-month prison term. IPCO ruled, however, that there was ultimately no error made as defined by the IPA. “This is because the activity was lawfully authorised under an interception warrant and the adoption of an unintentionally and unforeseeably imperfect target discovery methodology did not constitute such an error,” the report stated. Despite the agency’s vast technical expertise, IPCO said that the issue affecting the software was not foreseeable. GCHQ was not the only offender among the UK intelligence community (UKIC), with MI5's mishandling of the infamous Agent X case taking center stage in the report. Agent X was an anonymous MI5 informant whose real identity has never been publicly released. A secret inquiry by IPCO as well as the report revealed that MI5 managed Agent X despite knowing he was a violent misogynist obsessed with extreme violence. Lord Leveson said "the case of Agent X is as serious as anything I have dealt with as Commissioner," after MI5 gave false evidence to the High Court and Investigatory Powers Tribunal to protect a foreign neo-Nazi informant who was under police investigation for abusing his partner, referred to publicly as "Beth." ®

item.title: Accenture AI agents are sifting through applicants
item.description: Accenture is using AI across its recruiting process, although it maintains that final hiring decisions remain in human hands. Speaking to at its recent investor day, the global tech consultancy and outsourcing biz said it was using AI agents to sift through resumes (or CVs if you’re in the UK) and schedule interviews. Kate Clifford, global chief leadership and HR, said it was helping clients adopt a similar application of the nascent technology. "We call it frictionless recruiting, which is really our agentic recruiting solution. We put in an agentic recruiting solution where agents now do all the interview scheduling. Agents can screen a resume. We have assessments that deeply understand the skills of the candidates to help that process move much, much faster. Now a human always makes a hiring decision," she said. Clifford said the agent technology was used to help recruitment staff get through their work more quickly. "Our recruiters needed to spend time with candidates. They needed to spend time sourcing, but where they were actually spending their time was scheduling interviews, where they were actually spending their time was typing information into a system," she said. The executive claimed the agentic process reduced the time taken to hire for roles by 28 percent and improved candidate quality by 30 percent. AI agents also help new recruits get up to speed. Whereas it once took six months for an entry-level hire to become productive, the time has been cut to six weeks using AI agents, Clifford claimed, allowing them to produce billable work more rapidly. Accenture claims to serve around 9,000 clients — including some of the world’s largest businesses and government departments — with tech advice and services. For example, it won a contract with the US Internal Revenue Services worth $2.6 billion in 2023 . Any tech pro looking for a job with the company is likely being screened by AI as part of the process. The company also expects internal staff to get on the AI bandwagon. A memo sent to senior staff in February informed them that promotions to top roles at the corporation would necessitate "regular adoption" of AI tooling, and it is tracking usage. But not everyone is convinced by the value of AI in recruitment. A study published in 2022 found the idea that AI-powered recruitment software creates a fairer process was unfounded. A paper published in the journal Philosophy and Technology demonstrated that the software is little more than "automated pseudoscience." Tech job-hunters applying for a lucrative role at Accenture will be hoping the technology has moved on since then. ®

Clifford said the agent technology was used to help recruitment staff get through their work more quickly. "Our recruiters needed to spend time with candidates. They needed to spend time sourcing, but where they were actually spending their time was scheduling interviews, where they were actually spending their time was typing information into a system," she said. The executive claimed the agentic process reduced the time taken to hire for roles by 28 percent and improved candidate quality by 30 percent. AI agents also help new recruits get up to speed. Whereas it once took six months for an entry-level hire to become productive, the time has been cut to six weeks using AI agents, Clifford claimed, allowing them to produce billable work more rapidly. Accenture claims to serve around 9,000 clients — including some of the world’s largest businesses and government departments — with tech advice and services. For example, it won a contract with the US Internal Revenue Services worth $2.6 billion in 2023 . Any tech pro looking for a job with the company is likely being screened by AI as part of the process. The company also expects internal staff to get on the AI bandwagon. A memo sent to senior staff in February informed them that promotions to top roles at the corporation would necessitate "regular adoption" of AI tooling, and it is tracking usage. But not everyone is convinced by the value of AI in recruitment. A study published in 2022 found the idea that AI-powered recruitment software creates a fairer process was unfounded. A paper published in the journal Philosophy and Technology demonstrated that the software is little more than "automated pseudoscience." Tech job-hunters applying for a lucrative role at Accenture will be hoping the technology has moved on since then. ®

item.title: Think Halloween is scary? This scorched alien world is a real-life cosmic horror story
item.description: null Earth would be terrifying if we celebrated Halloween every 11 hours, a possibility on a super-Earth investigated by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). That is, if this extrasolar planet, or exoplanet, wasn't so hellishly hot that no life could survive on its surface. The exoplanet in question is the rocky lava planet TOI-561 b, located around 280 light-years away, which was discovered by NASA's exoplanet-hunting spacecraft TESS (Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite) in 2020. The planet is located so close to its star, TOI-561, that not only does it complete an orbit every 11 hours, but its surface temperatures reach in excess of 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit (1,800 degrees Celsius). That is so hot that astronomers once believed that TOI-561 b couldn't possibly possess an atmosphere. With 37 hours of JWST observations covering nearly four full orbits of TOI-561, scientists have now found this horrific planet is buried in a reflective layer of vaporized silicate mineral clouds, the same family of compounds that make up quartz and sand. "We measured how the planet's brightness and heat changed throughout its orbit," team member Lisa Dang of the University of Waterloo said in a statement. "This technique, known as a phase curve, revealed that the planet reflects a significant amount of light from its star, and that heat is being redistributed around the planet instead of only on the sunlit side. Together, these point to the presence of an atmosphere." The hemispheres of lava super-Earth are day and night The proximity of TOI-561 b to its star has another consequence. The planet is tidally locked, meaning it doesn't turn like Earth . Thus, TOI-561 b has one blisteringly hot "dayside" permanently facing its star, and a cooler "nightside" facing out into space in perpetuity. Dang and colleagues investigated the fact that the bare rock of the dayside seemed to be cooler than should be expected. They theorized that missing heat could be carried around to the night side or the heat may be reflected away before TOI-561 b can absorb it. By using the JWST to observe full orbits of TOI-561 b, the team was able to observe the planet's nightside for the first time. They found it isn't warm enough to account for all the heat missing from the dayside. That means TOI-561 b must reflect roughly three-quarters of the starlight that hits it. That is comparable to the most reflective planet in the solar system, Venus , which reflects around 75% of incident sunlight compared to the 30% reflected by Earth. The team determined that this high reflectivity is the result of clouds of silicate minerals, including silicon dioxide and magnesium silicate, forming on the planet's dayside and acting like sunscreen. These clouds could also help TOI-561 b hang on to an atmosphere. A diagram shows that TOI-561 b and its two exoplanet siblings would fit well within the orbit of Mercury around the sun (Image credit: NASA) Of course, the team can't yet be sure what this atmosphere

The team determined that this high reflectivity is the result of clouds of silicate minerals, including silicon dioxide and magnesium silicate, forming on the planet's dayside and acting like sunscreen. It could be a dense carbon dioxide fog like that seen on Venus, or it could be a blanket of sulfur dioxide like that of the most volcanic body in the solar system, Jupiter's moon Io . That would be the case if, like on Io, volcanic activity is replenishing the atmosphere of TOI-561 b. "The next big question we will seek to answer is whether TOI-561 b's atmosphere resembles Venus or an extreme version of Io," Dang said. "Observing the planet at longer wavelengths with JWST could give us insights and help explain how a planet this hot has held on to an atmosphere for billions of years." The team's research was published in The Astronomical Journal.

item.title: Can We Talk About Tenicka Boyd’s Lagos Fashion Week Style?
item.description: The American fashion influencer, whose effortlessly polished approach to dressing has earned her a devoted following, has been turning heads in Lagos with a wardrobe that’s equal parts playful and unapologetically sophisticated. And if there’s one thing her appearances have made clear, it’s that Boyd understands the assignment when it comes to fashion week. Scroll through Tenicka Boyd ’s standout Lagos Fashion Week looks below. Tenicka Boyd/Instagram For her Jewel Jemila appearance, Boyd embraced full-on romance in a sweeping fuchsia dress, complete with cascading ruffles and dramatic bell sleeves. Paired with gold jewellery and her signature sleek, centre-parted hair, the look was a masterclass in polished style. Tenicka Boyd/Instagram She switched gears for Beverly Naya ’s Skin Summit experience, opting for a striking black-and-white body-skimming dress with an abstract, zebra-inspired pattern and dramatic fringe detailing. Tenicka Boyd/Instagram But perhaps her most playful look came courtesy of The LadyMaker. Tenicka Boyd/Instagram Boyd paired a sculptural hot-pink puff-sleeve top with a voluminous orange bubble skirt, finishing the look with a purple tasseled handbag and coordinating heels. Tenicka Boyd/Instagram And then there’s this insanely detailed Onalaja burgundy beaded ensemble, a rich, intricately embellished look that traded playful volume for texture and craftsmanship, reinforcing Boyd’s ability to move between different fashion moods without losing her distinct point of view. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Tenicka (@tenickab) Beyond the clothes, Boyd’s Lagos emphasizes the growing visibility of African designers on the global fashion stage. For an influencer whose wardrobe regularly spans international luxury houses and emerging labels, we love that her enthusiasm for Nigerian fashion feels like a natural extension of her personal style. And with looks this good, we’re definitely paying attention. *** Photography: Ayo Makinwa The post Can We Talk About Tenicka Boyd’s Lagos Fashion Week Style? appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Patrick Stewart, renowned actor and ‘Star Trek’s’ Captain Picard, dies at 86
item.description: null Less than a week after the fates took Walter Koenig from our galaxy, another " Star Trek " legend has left us: Sir Patrick Stewart has died at the age of 86. According to his spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak, the beloved Shakespearean actor passed away on Wednesday (Oct. 28) at his Los Angeles home after a short struggle with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia. "He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all," Bush Novak shared. "We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace." Patrick Stewart in director John Boorman's spectacular film, "Excalibur." (Image credit: Warner Bros.) The first time I ever saw Patrick Stewart was in director John Boorman’s masterful 1981 King Arthur film, "Excalibur." As a young teenager, I was immediately captivated by his commanding presence and charisma portraying King Leodegrance of Cameliard — Queen Guinevere’s noble father and a cunning warrior. In 1984, he entered the sci-fi realm in David Lynch's grand and ambitious adaptation of Frank Herbert's "Dune," in which he played Paul Atreides' good friend and mentor, War Master Gurney Halleck. Patrick Stewart in David Lynch's "Dune" from 1984. (Image credit: Universal Pictures) Stewart was later cast as the U.S.S. Enterprise’s Capt. Jean-Luc Picard in " Star Trek: The Next Generation . He entranced millions of viewers in this role, traveling the final frontier with his gallant crew and redefining the brave and compassionate traits of a Federation starship commander. His adventurous journey on that popular show, a spinoff of "Star Trek: The Original Series," ran from 1987 to 1994, encompassing 178 episodes across seven seasons confronting Klingons, Cardassians, Romulans and The Borg. When the series ended, Stewart continued on in the Enterprise's center seat by starring in four "Star Trek" feature films: 1994’s "Star Trek: Generations," 1996’s "Star Trek: First Contact," 1998’s "Star Trek: Insurrection," and 2002’s "Star Trek: Nemesis." Stewart also reprised the role of Jean-Luc Picard in three seasons of Paramount+’s " Star Trek: Picard ," which ran from 2020 to 2023. Stewart's prodigious talent was on further display in the hit adaptations of Marvel’s " The X-Men ." He played the powerful, wheelchair-bound telepath Professor Charles Xavier in 2000’s "X-Men," 2003’s "X2: X-Men United," 2006’s "X-Men: The Last Stand," 2014’s "X-Men: Days of Future Past," and 2017’s "Logan." Stewart, and Xavier, were prominently featured in those films. The actor and character also appeared in 2009’s "X-Men Origins: Wolverine" and 2013’s "The Wolverine," and will do so again in " Avengers: Doomsday ," which will be released around Christmastime this year. Aside from the two "Star Trek" and "The X-Men" franchise roles, Stewart had a flourishing career

His adventurous journey on that popular show, a spinoff of "Star Trek: The Original Series," ran from 1987 to 1994, encompassing 178 episodes across seven seasons confronting Klingons, Cardassians, Romulans and The Borg. When the series ended, Stewart continued on in the Enterprise's center seat by starring in four "Star Trek" feature films: 1994’s "Star Trek: Generations," 1996’s "Star Trek: First Contact," 1998’s "Star Trek: Insurrection," and 2002’s "Star Trek: Nemesis." Stewart's prodigious talent was on further display in the hit adaptations of Marvel’s " The X-Men ." He played the powerful, wheelchair-bound telepath Professor Charles Xavier in 2000’s "X-Men," 2003’s "X2: X-Men United," 2006’s "X-Men: The Last Stand," 2014’s "X-Men: Days of Future Past," and 2017’s "Logan." Stewart, and Xavier, were prominently featured in those films. The actor and character also appeared in 2009’s "X-Men Origins: Wolverine" and 2013’s "The Wolverine," and will do so again in " Avengers: Doomsday ," which will be released around Christmastime this year. Aside from the two "Star Trek" and "The X-Men" franchise roles, Stewart had a flourishing career that spanned radio, stage and screen and was always a stellar attraction at any comic-con or other fan event around the world. Another of his many memorable projects was the compelling one-man stage show in which he played all the characters in Charles Dickens' novella "A Christmas Carol," captured on a two-disc CD set that I listen to each holiday season. Patrick Stewart played the telepathic Professor Charles Xavier in the popular "X-Men" movies. (Image credit: 20th Century Studios) Knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010, Sir Patrick Stewart leaves behind a remarkable legacy that brought a rare gravitas and humanity to every performance he was ever involved in, and his passing leaves fans, friends and loved ones with heavy hearts. Here’s to a wonderful life well-lived!

item.title: On this day in space! Oct. 29, 1991: NASA's Galileo spacecraft flies by asteroid Gaspra and snaps amazing photos while flying at 18,000 mph
item.description: null On Oct. 29, 1991, the Galileo spacecraft flew by the asteroid Gaspra on its way to Jupiter. Gaspra was the first asteroid to ever be visited by a spacecraft. Gaspra orbits near the inner edge of the asteroid belt . The Galileo spacecraft had been travelling through the asteroid belt for about two months before it reached Gaspra. Galileo was 990 miles (1,593 kilometers) away from Gaspra when it whizzed by, and it was travelling at a relative speed of about 5 miles (8 km) per second. The spacecraft took several photos of the asteroid and used an instrument called the Near-Infrared Mapping Spectrometer to study its chemical composition and other physical properties. Galileo determined that Gaspra has an irregular and elongated shape measuring about 12 miles long and 7 miles wide. The images revealed that Gaspra was also covered in craters. Because Galileo was too far away for Gaspra's gravity to affect it, the spacecraft was not able to determine the asteroid's mass. A closeup view of asteroid Gaspra from NASA's Galileo spacecraft, which flew by the asteroid on the way to Jupiter. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Why it mattered The Galileo spacecraft's flyby of Gaspra was a pitstop near the midpoint of its 6-year journey to Jupiter, the largest planet in our solar system. NASA launched Galileo toward Jupiter in October 1989, with the probe swinging by Venus and Earth in 1990 before its encounter with Gaspra. The Gaspra flyby was the first asteroid flyby in history, with Galileo approaching to just under 1,000 miles (1,601 kilometers) while flying at a whopping 18,000 mph. Galileo's photos of Gaspra "revealed a cratered, complex, irregular body about 20 by 12 by 11 kilometers (12.4 by 7.4 by 6.8 miles), with a thin covering of dust and rubble," NASA wrote in an overview . "The picture we get of Gaspra is one of something that has suffered a lot during its history," the UPI press service quoted Joseph Veverka, a Galileo imaging team member, as saying at the time . "We suspect that this is the survivor of a series of catastrophic collisions in the past." An artist's conception of the Galileo spacecraft, which was launched in 1989 for a mission to Jupiter. (Image credit: NASA) Galileo would go on to fly by Earth a second time in 1992, then swing close by the asteroid Ida in 1993 before finally arriving at Jupiter in 1995. Along the way, the probe was in the right place at the right time to watch as the Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 broke into pieces and crashed into Jupiter in July 1994. Since Galileo's historic first asteroid flyby, NASA and other space agencies have gone on to land on asteroids (like NEAR on asteroid Eros ), collect samples of asteroids and return them to Earth (like NASA's OSIRIS-REx and Japan's Hayabusa probes), and have even intentionally crashed probes into asteroids (like NASA's DART asteroid impact mission ) to test planetary protection techniques. item.title: Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman named deputy director for NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory
item.description: null The leader of NASA's first mission around the moon in half a century is the last to announce what's next for him after retiring from active astronaut duty. All four astronauts of the Artemis II mission, which flew around the moon in April, have hung up their spacesuits and moved on to greener pastures. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), managed by Caltech, announced yesterday that former NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman will step into the role of Caltech associate vice president and deputy director of JPL, beginning Nov. 30. "Reid has spent his career at the edge of what is possible, and he has the technical judgment, operational experience, and leadership to help push that edge farther," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a JPL press release . Wiseman announced his transition to "astronaut emeritus" alongside Artemis II pilot Victor Glover in September. Glover, subsequently, accepted a full-time role as executive advisor to the president of his alma mater , California Polytechnic State University (Cal Poly). Artemis II mission specialists, Christina Koch and Canada's Jeremy Hansen , also made the decision to step away from their spaceflight careers. Hansen announced his career change in July, and has since entered into reservist duty with the Royal Canadian Air Force. Koch, more recently, was appointed as NASA's acting deputy chief engineer, effective Nov. 1. The quartet launched aboard NASA's Orion capsule on April 1, and completed a 10-day flight around the far side of the moon and back. item.dc:creator: Josh Dinner
item.content:encoded: null The leader of NASA's first mission around the moon in half a century is the last to announce what's next for him after retiring from active astronaut duty. All four astronauts of the Artemis II mission, which flew around the moon in April, have hung up their spacesuits and moved on to greener pastures. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), managed by Caltech, announced yesterday that former NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman will step into the role of Caltech associate vice president and deputy director of JPL, beginning Nov. 30. "Reid has spent his career at the edge of what is possible, and he has the technical judgment, operational experience, and leadership to help push that edge farther," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a JPL press release . Wiseman announced his transition to "astronaut emeritus" alongside Artemis II pilot Victor Glover in September. Glover, subsequently, accepted a full-time role as executive advisor to the president of his alma mater , California Polytechnic State University (Cal Poly). Artemis II mission specialists, Christina Koch and Canada's Jeremy Hansen , also made the decision to step away from their spaceflight careers. Hansen announced his career change in July, and has since entered into reservist duty with the Royal Canadian Air Force. Koch, more recently, was appointed as NASA's acting deputy chief engineer, effective Nov. 1. The quartet launched aboard NASA's Orion capsule on April 1, and completed a 10-day flight around the far side of the moon and back. Their mission took them further from Earth than any crewed spaceflight in history, and captured the attention of millions, who were captivated by the astronauts' incredible views and their ability to demonstrate the best traits of humanity, even while being the four people farthest from it. The mission served as a stepping stone in NASA's Artemis program which aims to return astronauts to the surface of the moon and eventually establish a permanent base there. NASA is targeting mid-2027 for Artemis III as a flight test with Orion and the two Artemis lunar lander spacecraft (SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon ). If everything goes according to plan, that mission will pave the way for Artemis IV, and the program's first crewed lunar landing in 2028. From left: The Artemis II crew — NASA astronaut Christina Koch, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen, and NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Victor Glover — take time out for a group hug inside the Orion spacecraft on April 6, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) A Baltimore native, Wiseman is a retired U.S. Navy captain who served as an aviator and test pilot before joining NASA's astronaut corps in 2009. He launched to space for the first time on the on the Soyuz TMA-13M mission to the International Space Station (ISS). He spent 165 days in orbit serving as part of ISS Expeditions 40 and 41, and completed two spacewalks totaling nearly 13 hours. Before his selection for Artemis II, Wiseman worked as NASA's chief astronaut, overseeing crew readiness, astronaut assignments and flight safety from Dec. 2020 - Nov. 2022. As JPL's new deputy director, Wiseman will serve under Director Dave Gallagher, helping oversee "strategic leadership, stewardship, and continuous improvement of laboratory operations," according to the JPL release. JPL is a federally funded research and development center specializing in robotic space exploration. The lab is responsible for some of NASA's most recognizable planetary missions, including the Perseverance and Curiosity Mars rovers, Europa Clipper and the Voyager probes. JPL also operates NASA's Deep Space Network, which provides continuous communications with spacecraft throughout the solar system. "I've explored the furthest reaches of what a human can explore at NASA — and there were truly no words in the English vocabulary to describe seeing the sun disappear behind the moon from deep space," Wiseman said. "But that experience was really the jumping off point to go do the impossible things that Caltech and JPL dream, dare together, and do for NASA and the nation.”

item.title: Astronauts deploy solar array on 100th US spacewalk by International Space Station crew members
item.description: null Two astronauts successfully installed and deployed the second-to-last upgraded solar array for the International Space Station (ISS) during the 100th U.S. spacewalk from the orbiting outpost. Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency (CSA), both ISS Expedition 75 crewmates, completed the 7-hour-and-11-minute extravehicular activity (EVA) at 3:08 p.m. EDT (1908 GMT) on Thursday (Oct. 29). The spacewalk began and ended inside the U.S. Quest airlock, with both astronauts wearing NASA's extravehicular mobility unit (EMU) spacesuits. It was the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut since April 2019, when David Saint-Jacques ventured into the void with NASA's Anne McClain. NASA astronaut Anil Menon carries a rolled-up solar array to the site where it will be deployed while riding on the end of the Canadarm robotic arm during a spacewalk outside the International Space Station on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) Once outside, Menon and Kutryk worked on unbolting the ISS roll-out solar array ( iROSA ) from a temporary stowage platform. The 10-by-2-by-4-foot (3-by-0.6-by-1.2-meter) rolled-up assembly was delivered to the space station inside the unpressurized trunk of SpaceX 's Dragon cargo capsule earlier this month, on the company's 35th ISS resupply mission for NASA. Menon then secured himself at the end of the Canadarm2 robotic arm and carried the 750-pound (340-kilogram) iROSA to the space station's port side, where he and Kutryk next installed it on the 2A electrical power channel. Kutryk made his way to the worksite along the station's backbone truss. Using bolts to mount the IROSA in place and connecting its electrical cables to tie it into the station's power system (during a night pass, out of safety concerns), the array was ready to be extended. No motor was needed to deploy the iROSA to its 63-foot (19-m) length. The potential energy held by the assembly's rolled-up carbon composite booms was enough to fully unroll the panel. "And we see the iROSA deploying now," reported Mission Control four hours and 23 minutes into the spacewalk. About 12 minutes later, the array had fully extended, draping over about half of the larger but less capable legacy panel on the P4 truss. The station's eight original arrays are showing degraded power output as they have exceeded their 15-year design life. The iROSAs, when used in tandem with their older counterparts, have increased the station's power supply by 20% to 30%. The additional power is needed to support ongoing and planned station operations, including its safe and controlled deorbit , which is currently scheduled for 2030. Having worked ahead of their schedule, Menon and Kutryk removed some of the beams holding the final iROSA in place on its temporary platform and rotated two launch locks that were used in its delivery on Dragon . Thursday's EVA was the 100th U.S. outing from the space station without a now-retired space shuttle docked to the complex. Overa
